talks.title: Keynote Panel I: Imperialism Today. Palestine, Iran and Beyond
talks.abstract:
With Jamila Mascat, Mikki Stelder, Joseph Daher and Kayhan Valadbaygi.

Mikki Stelder is an Assistant Professor of Global Arts and Politics at the University of Amsterdam. Their research and writing bring together anticolonial thought, queer transfeminist politics, international law, and Palestine liberation. Their forthcoming book, Contract Colonialism, examines the colonial legal thought of Hugo Grotius and its afterlives in structures of violence, dispossession, and extraction.

Joseph Daher is an internationalist, anticapitalist and an academic. He teaches at Lausanne University and is a part time affiliate professor at the European University Institute, Florence (Italy). He is the author of Syria after the Uprisings (Pluto, 2019), Hezbollah: The Political Economy of Lebanon’s Party of God (Pluto, 2016), Palestine and Marxism (Resistance Books, 2024). He is the founder of the blog Syria Freedom Forever.

Kayan Valadbaygi is a Research Fellow at the International Institute of Social History (IISH) in Amsterdam and CEO of Middle East Risk & Reform Advisory. He is the author of Capitalism in Contemporary Iran: Capital Accumulation, State Formation and Geopolitics (Manchester University Press, 2024).

talks.title: Politics, Social Movements and Scientific Publishing: A Dialogue
talks.abstract:
In the Netherlands, there are several academic journals with a distinct left-wing orientation. Although active in different fields of research, these journals share aims, questions, challenges and dilemmas — and rarely have the occasion to reflect on these together with each other, their authors and their audiences. This roundtable brings together editors involved in journals historically rooted in, or adjacent to, social movements and Marxist projects to discuss the future of socially committed research and publishing. 

The roundtable will foreground concrete experiences, policies and practices as much as theoretical concerns, and will take the following topics as a starting point:
•	**Neoliberal academia**: The impact of neoliberal policies on the academic landscape, resulting in an emphasis on rankings, excellence and quantifiable impact. What do these changes mean for socially committed journals and researchers—and how have socially committed publication initiatives navigated their impact? 
•	**Academic norms and social commitment**: What does it mean for a journal today to balance the expectations that come with a claim to the “academic,” on the one hand, and social accountability on the other? How have the journals navigated demands of academic legitimacy or ‘neutrality’ while retaining accountability towards the movements and emancipatory struggles in which their work is rooted?
•	**Right-wing politics**: How do current political changes affect socially committed research and publishing? To what extent have the journals positioned themselves explicitly in relation to resurgent right-wing politics, and to what extent do they experience concrete effects stemming from the rise of the far right and a general political dominance of right-wing parties?
•	**Movements**: The role of scholars and journals in relation to current-day and past historical movements. How have academic journals contributed to movements in the past, and how can they do so in the future?

The following speakers will kick off the discussion:
•	Joost Kircz of Marxism & Sciences (confirmed)
•	Louis Hartnoll of Historical Materialism (confirmed)
•	Josie Läuferts of Jaarboek voor de Geschiedenis van Arbeidersbewegingen en Socialisme in Nederland (confirmed)
•	Margo de Koster of Brood & Rozen (confirmed)
•	Owen Worth of Capital and Class (confirmed)
•	Tivadar Vervoort of Krisis (confirmed)
•	Chair: Rosa Kösters

We see this roundtable as an urgent opportunity for collective reflection during a moment when both the academic landscape and the broader political environment are shifting rapidly. Together with all participants in the room, we aim to discuss shared experiences, probe common tensions and chart potential paths forward.

talks.title: Extraction and Absorption: Metabolic Rift at Sea in the Works of Minerva Cuevas and Kelly Jazvac
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract: Being submersed in the Capitalocene is like being out at sea with no land in sight — the totality of capitalist abstraction has made our relations to one another and to the planet increasingly opaque. In this talk, I will demonstrate art’s unique ability to locate and visualize conditions that have become increasingly inaccessible in this hazy, ever-moving landscape, with a particular focus on the artistic practices of Minerva Cuevas and Kelly Jazvac. Cuevas and Jazvac, in their respective works, _Horizon II_ (2016) and _Plastiglomerates_ (2013 - 2017), offer uncanny images of the consequences of Real abstraction, envisioning a social ecology overextracted, coughing up waste in the form of both literal trash and repressed colonial traumas. Through these artists’ practices and drawing from waste theory, particularly Métis scientist and ecological theorist Max Liboiron’s research on the history and implications of assimilative capacity as a framework for thinking about aquatic survival in the Capitalocene, I intend to extend Marxist analyses of the past two decades on the subject of metabolic rift, from land to sea. I will discuss what the ocean, too often seen as a source for endless extraction (ex. deep sea mining, overfishing, etc.) and absorption (ex. of plastic waste, oil spills, and bodies, as was the case during the atrocities of the transatlantic slave trade, for example, etc.), looks like under these conditions of rift. Ultimately, this talk will ask how the ocean and its depictions allow us to diagnose the consequences of capitalism’s endless externalization and reincorporation of the so-called Natural world for maximal extraction and, in turn, consider how artists such as Cuevas and Jazvac might help us map ways out of this crisis.

talks.title: Production Without Labor? AI and the Ruse of Subsumption in the Language Economy
talks.abstract:
Can the algorithmic training of neural networks fully model, and hence substitute, all human labor? How does the current proliferation of large language models (LLMs) relate to the scientific management of the division of labor and what Marx called the “real subsumption of labor by capital”? Since Alan Turing’s postulation of a “universal machine” that reduced all formal reasoning to symbol manipulation, modern computer science has increasingly operationalized the assumption that “human beings can be ‘Turing machines’ that follow rules,” and that all “productive processes” may thus be regarded “irrespective of the physical construction of the subject of the process” (Caffentzis 159). Linking the algorithmic epistemology of contemporary capitalism to the _longue durée_ of industrial modernity, Matteo Pasquinelli argues that contemporary AI represents “the culmination of the long evolution of labour automation and quantification of society” (247). Similarly, historian of science Lorraine Daston contends that “the history of calculation” is inseparable from “the history of work and machines” and “how mathematical algorithms intersected with political economy during the Industrial Revolution” (7-8). 

This paper seeks to both extend and put pressure on this socio-historical perspective. While locating the roots of the modern AI project in the industrial subsumption of labor helps dispel prevalent myths about a technology poised to remove human intervention from vast swathes of the global economy, this line of analysis has not yet sufficiently attended to the specifically linguistic character of LLMs. As Leif Weatherby has convincingly shown, while AI chatbots like ChatGPT are no more than “an algorithm and some data, a very large matrix that captures some linguistic structure,” they also represent “the deepest synthesis of word and number to date, and they require us to train our theoretical gaze on this interface” (8). Accordingly, this paper proposes that a Marxist theory of artificial intelligence must foreground the linguistic nature of generative AI and its connection to what Christian Marazzi called the “language economy” at the dawn of the new century. Rather than fulfilling capital’s old dream of production without labor, the contemporary rise of LLMs represents, more precisely, the technical formalization of linguistic labor required to make language use discrete, computable, and hence, amenable to (as with previously industrialized domains of production) capital’s valorization process. This reframing has significant implications for our understanding of the current trajectory of capitalist development as a form of Taylorization of the realm of signs.

talks.title: On the state of the transatlantic bargain
talks.abstract: Last year, I wrote an [article ]([url](https://www.tni.org/en/article/a-transatlantic-bargain))for the Transnational Institute on the structural reasons for, history, and continuity of Europe's submission to the United States. In the conclusion, I mention that it is by no means certain that the EU will want to hitch itself to an ever more crisis-ridden US global project but that structural reasons make this a difficult task. I want to revisit the US-European relation now that the crisis of US empire becomes ever more clear. I want to focus on the current state of NATO, the state of transatlantic financial and trade flows after two years of Trump's disruption, and on whether any ideological alternative to Atlanticism/submission to the US seems to be emerging in Europe.

talks.title: Against “Nature” as an abstract origin: towards a materialist concept of nature.
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract: ‘Nature’ as a function of philosophical discourse appears to be essential to the structure of the critique of capitalism and the critique of environmental degradation. By ‘nature’ as a function of discourse, we wish not primarily to direct attention to nature-as-ecosystem but rather to the abstract ideas used to legitimise a foundation in a pre-discursive naturalness: human nature, natural right, and finally “nature” as an essentialised denomination for ecosystems, species, and geophysical formations external to “culture” and the realm of humankind that it designates. Whether it is predicated on a humanist understanding of history, like Marxist humanism that centers its discourse on an abstract human subject, or a more inclusive posthumanist understanding of subjecthood – a lot of environmentalist critique relies on an abstract ‘natural’ substance as the ultimate cornerstone of its critical standpoint. The Althusserian reading of Marx remains to this date one of the most systematic attempts at thinking independently of any such foundational abstractions. It has notoriously vouched for “theoretical anti-humanism”: the attempt to produce a knowledge of social formations that is not articulated from the starting point of a concept of an abstract human “nature”. Yet, it seems implausible that environmental critique can fully do away with a reference to “Nature” – insofar as it is to critique the capitalist mode of production as the root cause of environmental destruction, it needs to specify the object of that destruction. It needs to be able to think a material exteriority to capitalism, without the appeal to which it seems unlikely that its critique of capitalism would pertain specifically to the destruction of ecosystems and of the concrete conditions of the upkeep of life on Earth. How then, in a framework that has so radically tried to purge out abstract ideas and their use as quasi-metaphysical foundations of critique, can a materialist concept of “Nature” be elaborated on the only possible ground for objectivity (in Althusser’s interpretation): the structure of the capitalist mode of production? Our contribution seeks to narrow this problem while suggesting concrete elements of the Althusserian corpus that seem fertile for such an elaboration. Now, in a time wherein environmental critique seems to run into an impasse, the attempt to think the primacy of the concrete-real is ever more urgent in order to develop a Marxist environmental politics that concerns itself with the materiality of social practices.

talks.title: Raw Power: Alex Karp, AI, and the Rise of Technofascism
talks.abstract:
From the late 1970s until the 2010s, the technology industry largely embraced “progressive neoliberalism” (Fraser), a discourse framing technology as supportive of economic agency and tethered to crucial advancements in social welfare. While unquestionably capitalist in nature, this rhetoric was nevertheless nominally informed by the collectivist legacy of the counterculture movement, i.e., the Californian ideology (Barbrook and Cameron). However, in recent years, this narrative has been exchanged for an overtly reactionary discourse positioning technology as a force multiplier of state power and a means of restricting individual freedom.

As I contend, this transition inheres in a shift from the ameliorative, third-way rhetoric (Giddens) of
late capitalism—typified by such figures as Steve Jobs and George Soros—to an overtly conservative, statist, and authoritarian discourse celebrating capitalism’s inherent capacity to produce indignity and immiseration, particularly in the service of American empire. For many critics, this indicates an unequivocally fascist turn in global politics (Klein and Taylor, Toscano).

This paper examines Alex Karp, CEO and co-founder of defense startup Palantir, as a key agent of this technofascist shift. Looking to Karp’s The Technological Republic and Palantir’s 22-point manifesto (published in April of 2026), I analyze how the emerging rhetoric of technofascism embraces the “raw power” of technology and seeks to reframe it as a means of fortifying the state. I specifically investigate how Karp positions AI technology, which the company has operationalized to assist the United States and Israel in identifying (civilian) targets, as a means of “mastering our world” (Karp).

talks.title: The Centennial of Fritz Sternberg’s Der Imperialismus
talks.abstract: The German Marxist economist Fritz Sternberg published his main work, Der Imperialismus, one hundred years ago in 1926. This book revised Rosa Luxemburg’s theory of imperialism, according to which capitalism depends on expansion into non-capitalist regions and must inevitably collapse once all regions are subsumed by the capitalist mode of production. Sternberg highlighted countervailing factors such as global fluctuations in the industrial reserve army of labor (relative surplus population). He correlated a progressive decline in the industrial reserve army with the general tendency of the rate of profit to decline. Thus capitalism strives to maintain a permanent surplus population. Moreover, in this book Sternberg developed a theory of imperialist wars that anticipated his later ideas of war-preparation economy and truce economy [Waffenstillstandswirtschaft]. Sternberg was involved in a number of Marxist controversies during the interwar period, most notably with Henryk Grossmann. His politics would radicalize amid the political and economic crises of the late Weimar Republic, leading him to join the Socialist Workers’ Party of Germany (SAPD). He would even collaborate with Trotsky on an economic policy for the Fourth International. His politics would moderate again during his years in US exile and his postwar involvement in German Social Democracy. Still, his theory of imperialism would continue to influence later generations of Marxist economists, most notably Ernest Mandel. Sternberg’s theoretical intervention ranks in importance alongside those of Luxemburg, Bukharin, Lenin, Otto Bauer, and Grossmann, yet Der Imperialismus remains the only major Marxist theory of imperialism from that era not translated yet into English. Thus, I have agreed with Brill to translate it along with Sternberg’s reply to critics as part of the Historical Materialism book series. This paper will summarize Sternberg’s theory, contextualize it in interwar Marxist debates, comment on the translation project, and argue for the book’s relevance to our present age of renewed imperialist aggression and capitalist crisis.

talks.title: Milking the worker: On cow labor and milky materialism
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract: Thinking with water, liquidity and fluidity has become more and more popular the last years. Especially feminists with a focus on embodied philosophy, new materialism and posthumanism, such as Astrida Neimanis and Stacy Alaimo, have been building theories on these premises of liquid being, porosity and hydrofeminism. In this paper I will critically examine this 'hydrological turn', as Cecilia Chen, Janine Macleod, and Astrida Neimanis call it (2013), from a Marxist and Critical Animal Studies viewpoint. My focus will be on a specific liquid, namely cow milk, to provide me with a material interlocutor to bring these different strands of theory together. I will introduce Neimanis' work on liquidity from this angle of mammal milk and will counter this interpretation of liquidity through a Marxist understanding of animal labor with the help of Dinesh Wadiwel's work to argue that the metaphoric understanding of liquidity in Neimanis' work overshadows the material contradictions reproduced through animal labor. This framework of labor will allow me to understand how this capitalist ontological schema is reproduced in mammal milk. I will put forth a dialectical understanding of cow milk, exposing the limits of the hydrological turn for feminist discourse, as well as critical animal studies.

talks.title: The age of disavowal: New epistemic oppressions in the digital age
talks.abstract:
Studies about the intrusion in society of digital technologies have often highlighted the lack of transparency, or opacity, that surrounds their introduction. In this field, Zuboff’s work has linked this opacity with class divisions, linking the power of capitalist elites with the gate-keeping of a certain knowledge from the rest of society. An explanatory gap in Zuboff’s theory however lies in her account of the mechanisms driving this social opacity that prevents society from taking action. According to her, the tool used by the capitalist ‘hive’ to maintain power in this realm is simply negating  to others the access to a certain knowledge about new modes of production. However, Zuboff’s emphasis on the gate-keeping of knowledge inside a small capitalist class is inadequate: Factual knowledge about modes of production and reification of human experience in the digital age is available and explicitly recognised across social classes. What remains to be explained then, is how come this factual knowledge fails to translate into collective action.
	I argue that this explanatory gap can be bridged, using the concept of disavowal. The latter has a marked psychological component, and describes the phenomenon whereby factual knowledge of an event fails to reach the affective consciousness of individuals, thus failing to cause the appropriate (re)action. This psychoanalytical term has been used by Zupančič to explain the social reaction to climate change, and I argue that this concept fills in the lacune in Zuboff’s account - that is, it explains the mechanism that prevents class action, despite the availability of factual knowledge of the situation. Specifically, Zupančič highlights that disavowal comes between knowledge, belief, and reality, hence it does not preclude the availability, or even presence, of knowledge. Instead, disavowal modifies the nature of the phenomenon, recognising it as part of reality yet changing its character in a way that makes it fundamental, something to adapt to rather than to challenge. This concept is well-suited to bridge the explanatory gap in Zuboff’s theory. Disavowal at the individual level prevents class consciousness to be mobilised against the new threats posed by the capitalist exploitation through digital technologies. The implication of this analysis is that ‘raising awareness’ and education are likely not to be effective tools of class struggle, rather a deeper engagement with the availability of collective political imaginaries is needed.

talks.title: Westalgia, or the Literature of Imperial Exhaustion
talks.abstract:
What affects and genres, what cultural logics and dominants, cohere in an age of imperial exhaustion? 

Internet slop might be one answer to that question, but two others, this paper argues, are Westalgia and the literature of imperial exhaustion. While the former describes an affect traceable across the ideological political spectrum in many Western cultures, the latter nods to John Barth’s well-known 1967 essay on literary postmodernism to describe a prominent genre in the narrative culture of the twenty-first century United States. My paper draws on Marxist understandings of history and the work of Fredric Jameson to elucidate these two theoretical concepts, which I will illustrate with a diverse set of examples, ranging from fictional podcasts that were briefly popular in the 2010s to AI-generated Iranian “slopaganda,” Mario Vargas Llosa’s novel _The Dream of the Celt_ (2012) and Ta-Nehisi Coates, _The Message_ (2024).

Westalgia, my readings of these texts will demonstrate, names a cultural nostalgia for “the West” that predates by some years open acknowledgment of the West’s parochialization in an age of multipolarity. The literature of imperial exhaustion, meanwhile, is what you get when the self-referentiality and endless chains of signification that characterize a cultural logic that is still postmodern collide with an awareness that the imperial power of the US has reached its historical limits.

talks.title: Cloud as Means of Production
talks.abstract:
Cloud computing is the lifeline of contemporary internet. Developed in parallel to the platformization of social life, the cloud has changed the way in which digital infrastructure, and large communication systems more broadly, are deployed. In so doing, it has allowed an unprecedented power concentration among three players, who together control over 60% of the global cloud provision market: Amazon, Microsoft and Google. The development of Generative AI cannot be understood without cloud computing, and the cloud takes up a considerable amount of the capital invested in the AI sector. 

Yet, despite its centrality to world-wide digital systems, the cloud has received comparatively little attention from scholars, policymakers and activists. Developing radical alternatives to the current structure of digital markets, and by extension capital itself, requires a theory of the cloud that can be used to embed it into popular political projects. 

This paper seeks to contribute towards such goal by conceptualising the cloud as means of production. Emphasising the (over)determining role of social relations of production in the character of the cloud, the present contribution argues that the centrality that this infrastructure has acquired over the last two decades can be explained through three interrelated processes: 

1. Infrastructural fix: the cloud allowed a change in the organic composition of capital, centralising the provision of digital infrastructure in data centres and commodifying software, thereby centralising power among providers while giving agility to customers.
2. Changing regimes of accumulation: these changes in turn resulted in a shift in the capitalist regimes of accumulation. It allowed for monopolization of infrastructure provision, while also providing scalable tools for customers to engage in their own strategies of assetization. 
3. Historical conjunctures: such transformations were part of a wider series of conjunctures emerging from the recent structural crises of capitalism, namely the Great Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 Pandemic. In both cases, cloud infrastructures allowed a displacement of capital’s structuring contradictions through the mechanisms outlined above. 

Conceptualising the cloud as an unity of these processes helps break with purely technical approaches to alternative digital infrastructures, instead presenting it as a fundamentally political object whose transformation can only be achieved through a transformation of the social relations of production.

talks.title: Reading Capital Today
talks.abstract:
Reading Capital Workshop -- 

This would be a guide to how and why to read capital. In the last 2 years there has been a large increase in Capital reading groups in the Netherlands. Why read Capital today? And how should we read Capital today? 

This would be a social workshop style event that focuses on those who have read Capital as a group or who want to start their own Capital reading group. We will aim to think about the challenges of doing this, as well as the specific relevance that reading Capital might have in our current moment

talks.title: Marxism & Global Labour History
talks.abstract: Historically, Marxist thought and labour history have been intimately tied together. The earliest research on the conditions and struggles of the working class were spearheaded by Marxists and communists interested in finding strategic insights to politically promote the interests of the working class. Today, global labour history is the most dynamic field within labour history. It emerged out of labour history’s twofold crisis of a proclaimed end of the labour movement on the one hand and critiques made by postcolonial and feminist scholars on the other. As a result, global labour historians rarely engage openly and constructively with Marxism. Given the persistence of capitalist exploitation and crisis and the resurgence of interest in and practice of Marxist academic research in other disciplines over the last twenty years, it is timely to consider how Global Labour History and Marxism relate today. In this panel, we want to discuss how we can reinject Marxism as the critical social theory of Marxism, and as a political commitment into the research and practice of Global Labour History.

talks.title: Whose Intelligence? Data Workers and Global Struggle for Political Subjectivity in the AI Era
talks.abstract:
The rise of Generative Artificial Intelligence is commonly framed as a triumph of immaterial automation. However, the emergence of the Data Labelers Association is radically deconstructing this myth, exposing the class conflict that drives the digital supply chain. This paper centers its analysis on the active resistance of these workers, arguing that their collective organization represents the most significant challenge to the ideology of "ghost work."
Rather than merely submitting to the extractive regimes of data annotation and content moderation, the workers within the Data Labelers Association are emerging as political subjects, forcing open the "hidden abode of production" that the industry seeks to keep invisible. By examining their mobilization strategies, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of the "Digital Unconscious": it is no longer viewed merely as a spatial category of passive exploitation, but as the terrain of a frontal clash between the logic of algorithmic capital and the subjectivity of Global South workers.
Within this framework, so-called AI "hallucinations" are reinterpreted. They are not simply technical bugs, but points of political friction where living labor resists the probabilistic reduction of reality. The Data Labelers Association demonstrates that the industry's attempt to bridge the gap between computation and human truth through fragmented, underpaid labor is inherently unstable. By analyzing their struggles, the paper concludes that the true threat to the AI industry is not algorithmic error, but the material "return of the repressed": the emerging self-consciousness and political organization of those whose daily efforts prevent the machine from collapsing into nonsense.

talks.title: The Slave and the Machine: Coerced Labor and the Origins of Modern Technology
talks.abstract:
In 1869, in the wake of the Civil War and the abolition of slavery, the Louisiana inventor J. C. Delavigne boasted of the steam plow he had just patented. It was, he said, “an iron negro, that cannot be emancipated.” Well into the twenty-first century, industrialists and inventors would compare technological innovations to racialized and enslaved people. “Since we can’t have slaves or kick around black people anymore,” said the inventor of the first industrial robot in 1972, “the robot serves that purpose.” Speaking in 2024 of what his Optimus robot would one day achieve, Elon Musk claimed that it would become the equivalent of an ideal house slave. The robot, he has said, “will babysit your kids, walk your dog, mow your lawn, get the groceries, just be your friend, serve drinks—whatever you can think of, it will do. It’s going to be awesome.” No society of the past built into its concept of technology the idea that it should work like a slave. That idea is new to modernity. This paper will consider how coerced and racialized labor came to serve as a model for the development of modern technology.
    The modern understanding of technology is inextricable from the history and values of capitalism. Before industrialists could mechanize labor, they had to reconceive work itself; they needed to see it as something a machine could—and should—perform. The ability to think of work as an entity that was machine-processable was new to the industrial revolution and, in order to be considered commonsensical, required nothing short of a revolution in the way that moderns thought about labor. That conceptual revolution first took place on the slave plantations of the New World. There, owners experimented with the radical degradation of work. In the process, they reconceived labor as a linear sequence of discrete tasks—divided in detail, assigned to disempowered workers, mechanized, and powered by inanimate force. The factory system, this paper argues, would then become the model for the modern understanding of technology.

talks.title: The workplace as a contested terrain: The crisis of social reproduction in food work
talks.abstract: This paper explores the suitability of Labour Process Theory (LPT) for addressing the relationship between digital technologies and the crisis of social reproduction in food work. With Rao (2021: 41), we distinguish a crisis of social reproduction for capital that threatens accumulation from a related crisis of social reproduction for labour which bears the brunt of capitalists’ adjustment. The latter is rooted in processes of devaluation of reproductive work, widely labelled ‘essential work’ during the Covid-19 pandemic. Amidst argumentative poles that perceive digitalisation as either exacerbating work precarity (Moore 2019) or offering a ‘post-work model’ to solving the crisis of social reproduction (Hester and Srnicek 2017), our contribution asks whether novel digital technologies in essential sectors are addressing or amplifying these crises. LPT may offer a suitable approach to address this question because it understands the ‘workplace as a contested terrain’, which prevents it from advancing deterministic theses and counselling scepticism towards both optimistic and pessimistic scenarios of the role of digitalisation. The first part of our paper offers an analytical review rethinking the validity of LPT for working life in digitalised workplaces. We identify two relevant conceptual advances here. Firstly, Gandini (2019) introduces the concept of techno-normative control as a novel, digitally mediated form of labour control that combines the systematic use of technologies to evaluate and reward workers’ performance and exerts an indirect form of control by encouraging workers to internalize these metrics-driven norms (Omidi 2026: 182). Secondly, Steinhoff (2024: 215) contends that deskilling is best understood as a component of a process that Marx called ‘absorption’. It involves not only the extraction of capacities from labour but also their implementation in machines, a process that might ultimately enable a new dimension of Taylorism. The second part of our paper applies these conceptual tools to the analysis of food cultivation and processing, as an essential sector that has received scant attention in the literature on social reproduction despite its centrality to the reproduction of labour and life. First results of a review of existing literature feed scepticism both regarding the possibilities for full absorption of food workers’ knowledge in horticultural robotics as well as scant evidence of food workers’ resistance to the techno-normative control exerted through productivity monitoring software. Both findings imply ambivalence regarding the potential of digitalisation to revalue food work and underline the need for granular empirical work.

talks.title: The algorithmic logic: Gender inequalities in the intersection between reification (social objectification) and Artificial Intelligence (AI)
talks.abstract:
The emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is profoundly transforming social relations under contemporary capitalism. Drawing on a critical examination of György Lukács’s classic essay “Reification and the Consciousness of the Proletariat” (1923), this paper analyzes the intersection between the current global capitalist crisis, the general phenomenon of social reification, and the exponential development of artificial intelligence. To this end, it examines the consequences of these processes in the concrete terrain of gender inequalities.
From a classical Marxist perspective, the contradictory development of the productive forces under capitalism ultimately turns the worker into a “mere appendage” of the machine system, fragmenting and alienating the human experience. In Lukácsian terms, this expresses a process of social reification through which all human relations appear subordinated to mechanisms presented as objective, rational, and autonomous: in short, the commodification of the social metabolism.
We argue that the expansion of AI introduces a new logic into the social production of life, in which the algorithmic logic increasingly overlaps with the human logic, displacing socially alienated rationality with an alternative rationality. Human beings thus become dominated not only by the “natural” laws of capitalist social production, but also by the “artificial” laws generated through the widespread application of AI in every terrain of social life.
We contend that the growing replacement of human rationality (and rules) by the algorithmic logic of the AI has significant consequences for gender inequalities: (a) the differentiated impact on feminized occupations; (b) increased pressure on and invisibilization of care work and activities linked to social reproduction; (c) new forms of commodification of bodies, especially women’s bodies; and (d) the proliferation of deepfakes and the massive extraction of personal data, generating new forms of vulnerability and gender-based violence.

talks.title: Socialism and Associative Democracy
talks.abstract: The issue of the apt political form for a "democratic socialism" has been widely debated throughout the 20th century. In a recent book, Veit Bader and Marcel Maussen have presented a new approach, introducing and developing the idea of an "associative democracy" as an adequate political form for a self-organized, self-managed socialist economy. They have addressed most of the well-known issues that haunted the long debate on a feasible form of socialist self-government. Their plea for a diligent and meticulous approach to institution building for socialism deserves attention among the wider Marxist audience.

talks.title: Report on the Hartwig Foundation: Infrastructure and Antagonism in Dutch arts funding
talks.abstract:
This presentation will look critically at the [Hartwig Art Foundation]([url](https://www.hartwigartfoundation.nl/en)), a Dutch arts and culture institution founded by billionaire Rob Defares. The Foundation is currently building a major new museum in Amsterdam-Zuidas; it already has a temporary space (Hartwig Proxy) and funds many large scale projects and programmes. 
Our presentation will report on our research into the Hartwig Art Foundation, including its ties with state-political and Zionist actors, and its role within wider city and state policy.

We also look at some of the cultural projects supported by the Foundation (free workshops, cafes, ‘community choir’, etc), noting what Marina Vishmidt has described as the ‘gap between art institutions’ gestural benevolence and material violence’. 
Proxy has tended towards supporting projects proximate to participatory art/relational aesthetics, including ‘community’ cafes, workshops, choir; they also recently hosted RA darling, Rirkrit Tiravanija. We’re interested in what’s at stake in the return to this artistic tendency, thirty years after its inception (for critiques, see the work of Claire Bishop, Bojana Kunst, and Larne Abse Gogarty). Is this the same old story philanthropy, with its feel-good artwashing? What antagonisms are being covered over? What work are these aesthetic forms doing at this moment in history, and what about the other artistic projects Hartwig funds?
Our presentation draws on thinking from Vishmidt’s forthcoming book on infrastructural critique and considers how this might be applicable to a Dutch context, particularly in light of her suggestion to take the museum as _an infrastructure amenable to rearrangement through labour struggle._

To conclude, we reflect on recent turns to the category of the _art worker_, and the critiques on private and public arts funding, particularly in a Dutch context (see the work of Timo Demollin; cf Manchester’s [Commission for New and Old Art]([url](https://newleftreview.org/sidecar/posts/high-standards)),

talks.title: Too soft, too hard: internal change, gender, and left organizing
talks.track: Social reproduction, care and Marxist feminism
talks.abstract:
Too soft, too hard: internal change, gender, and left organizing 

Over the past few years, the psychic dimensions of resistance and societal change have been re-addressed in books such as Burn-out (2024) by Hannah Proctor and in a resurgence of psychoanalytic thinking on the left, exemplified by publications such as Parapraxis. Topics have included the need for internal change, group dynamics in organizing, and the medicalization of suffering under capitalism.
This talk enters these debates through the lens of gender. Debates around the psychological are inevitably gendered, as the psychological itself is gendered: the micro, local and intimate remain coded as feminine. Feelings remain coded as feminine. Social reproduction demands care, love, flexibility: tasks and values assigned to women. Conflict, militancy, and theory remain coded as masculine. For women in militant spaces, this creates a double bind: associated by default with softness, they risk embodying the ever-present danger of Marxism spiraling into liberalism.
Drawing on insights from my research on feminist critiques of psychiatry, I will explore how feminists have historically navigated this bind. One telling example: when feminists developed consciousness-raising practices, they were accused of “doing therapy”. This was despite the fact that these practices emerged as _critiques_ of therapy and resembled Marxist practices of criticism/self-criticism and “speaking bitterness”. In response, some feminists vehemently rejected the label; others asked: what is wrong with therapy? Some embraced feminine values; others disavowed care and told women to toughen up. I will argue that neither resolved the tension.
The terms of the bind seem to have shifted. Many feminists who disavowed care eventually returned, recognizing that dependency is inescapable. Today, many still insist on care, reparation, interrelatedness. But how radical is that in a context where liberalism speaks the language of empathy and connection? Where, if we believe Anna Kornbluh, immediacy, intimacy and affect without discourse have become the style of late capitalism? This talk asks how we can think about the psychic dimension of resistance, without getting stuck in the same old (gendered) impasses.

talks.title: 'Some are more peasant than others': essentalism and class dynamics in West African agroecology movements
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract:
In my presentation, I focus on the phenomenon of peasant essentialism within the agroecology movements of Senegal and Burkina Faso. Drawing on two case studies, I aim to illustrate importance of a materialist approach and a class lens for studying rural eco-movements.

Agroecology is becoming increasingly popular in both countries, where it is promoted by both grassroots food sovereignty networks and hegemonic development actors. A central development in the movements concerns the revaluation of ‘the peasant’. While French colonizers introduced the term with a derogatory connotation, actors assembling around agroecology (NGOs, research institutions, activist platforms, producer organizations, and individual producers) now reappropriate it to frame farmers as progressive and ecological protagonists.

While this rebranding may seem transformative, I argue that it has also a flipside, as the way key movement actors employ the concept of ‘the peasantry’ obscures power relations and class difference among rural labourers. Zooming in on two widely celebrated agroecology projects – a farm school in Senegal and a community development project in Burkina Faso- I demonstrate how the ‘model peasants’ in these flagship projects are affluent agropastoralists with privatized land ownership who can afford fenced infrastructures. First, I focus on the discursive level, namely the semiotic strategies used by the farmers, NGOs and donors to redefine the peasant as not a subsistence farmer who uses household labour but rather as a commerce-oriented farmer who employs the labour of others. I argue that this discursive shift obscures material difference. Second, I discuss the material effects produced and legitimized through this discourse: in both cases, the agroecological production models depend on the un(der)paid labour of landless others and on the enclosure of previously communal resources.

Drawing on the concept of ‘peasant essentialism’ from Marxist agrarian scholarship, I emphasize the importance of a class and labour lens for understanding these exploitation and expropriation dynamics in contemporary ecological movements. This lens allows us to focus on the differentiation and stratification among producers as they integrate into global capitalism in various ways. At the same time, the case studies illustrate the importance of an intersectional approach, as class and labour become meaningful categories of identity in relation to other aspects. 

More practically, the paper argues that to repoliticise agroecology and (re)align it with ambitions of climate justice, anticapitalism and anti-imperialism, the essentialist discourse on the peasantry needs to be problematized both in agroecology scholarship and practice.

talks.title: Free everyone right away: Aesthetics and Abolition
talks.abstract:
In this paper, I argue that the case of contemporary carceral expansion in the social democratic welfare state Denmark can serve as an entry point for grasping contemporary entanglements of welfare, care and coercion as drivers for carceral expansion, but that this demands an attention to aesthetic negotiation. Here, I engage with Marxist debates of the relationship between base and superstructure, bringing in Walter Benjamin’s comparison of this relationship with that of the sleeper, whose overfull stomach, even if it ‘conditions’ the dream, finds not its reflection, but its expression in the dream. Thinking with the productive aspects of the notion of expression in connection to poetry and music by artists such as Danish-Somali rapper Jamaika, from whom I borrow the title of this paper, I discuss how entering the analysis of carceral expansion from the point of aesthetic negotiations might enable the envisioning of what abolitionist Ruth Wilson Gilmore calls “liberatory lineages.”
Recently, abolitionist thinking has been mobilized in the fields of arts and cultural studies, especially in calls for the abolition of the bourgeois notion of art and its institutions (Maraud 2023, Catwings 2025, Routhier 2025). In his book, Die Überlegenheit der Unterlegenen (2024), Daniel Loick aims to formulate “[…] a general theory of the aesthetics of counter-communities.” Thinking with Peter Weiss’ aesthetics of resistance and Saidiya Hartman’s description of Black fugitive aesthetics, Loick argues that beauty here is located “not in harmony, but in conflict and struggle.” Drawing on Marxist aesthetic theory, as well as Black radicalism, this paper engages with these recent considerations of the connections between aesthetics and abolition but shifts the focus towards a question of the role of aesthetics in prison abolitionist analysis. How can we understand the role of aesthetics in abolitionist thinking and praxis, in opening an abolitionist horizon?
I situate these considerations in a contemporary context of an ongoing, radical expansion of the carceral system in Denmark. This expansion, I argue, is rooted in a racialization of the notion of crime and materializing in significant prison expansion and construction. The paper is part of a broader project, my PhD project with the working title Aestheticizing Incarceration (2025-2028). Using Stuart Hall et al.’s seminal Policing the Crisis (1978) as a methodological model, the project examines how an increase in the cultural presence of prison in contemporary Denmark intersects with the material expansion.

talks.title: The Question of the Proletarian Agent: Sex Work and the Limits of Marxism
talks.track: Social reproduction, care and Marxist feminism
talks.abstract: This paper examines the figure of the sex worker as a challenge to dominant Marxist theories of political agency. Within Marxist, feminist and leftist political traditions, sex workers have frequently been positioned as paradigmatic victims of exploitation while simultaneously being denied authority over the interpretation of their own labour. Through a reading of Marxist and Marxist-feminist theory alongside interviews with sex workers and sex worker writings, I argue that sex work exposes unresolved tensions in the construction of the proletarian subject and, by extension, the possibility of resistance. This paper reads sex workers as producers of political knowledge. Their accounts challenge familiar explanations based on false consciousness, coercion, and ideology, offering alternative understandings of agency grounded in contradiction, negotiation, and collective resistance. In this way, they reveal how certain Marxist approaches depend upon restricting workers' capacity to define their own interests and political practices. I propose that sex work functions as a critical lens through which to examine the limits of Marxist theories of consciousness, labour, and political subjectivity. The figure of the sex worker exposes tensions within existing conceptions of the proletarian agent, but also opens possibilities for rethinking agency from the standpoint of workers whose knowledge has historically been excluded from the left.

talks.title: Labour Environmentalism Against Industrial Pollution at the Hoogovens Steel Plant
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract: My paper explores the history of labour environmentalism through a case study of the Hoogovens steel plant in the Netherlands, focusing on the perspective of workers facing industrial pollution in their workplace. Histories of environmentalism are often closely tied to social struggles, a connection that has frequently been overlooked. Recent research has shown that the traditional 'jobs versus the environment trade-off' framework is flawed. Scholars are challenging the assumption that trade unions and workers did not engage with environmental issues because doing so conflicted with their interests in protecting their jobs and improving their wages (Barca 2024; Montrie 2018). In this case study, I discuss examples of workers and trade unions addressing environmental concerns and advocating for improved health and safety conditions throughout the history of the factory. My paper addresses the lack of in-depth analysis of labour environmentalism and coalitions between workers, trade unions and environmental groups within the Dutch context by exploring the struggles and coalitions involved in the case of the Hoogovens steel plant.

talks.title: Sex as a Political Problem, or Why Marxists Have To Think About Sex
talks.track: Social reproduction, care and Marxist feminism
talks.abstract: Lately we have seen a rise in arguments for economical change through arguments about better sex (for example ‘Why Women Under Socialism Have Better Sex’ by Kristen Ghodsee (2018) and ‘Rechts Verpest Onze Seks’ by Daan Borrel (2025)). Marxism does not need sex as an argument for social change – but this is also why it has not adequately theorized the role and form of sex within capitalist society. This paper analyses what a Marxist sex-positive account can look like. Political perspectives on sexuality can broadly be understood in three figures: 1) Sexuality as a repressed potential (Reich; Marcuse; Kollontai); 2) Sexuality as exploitation (Dworkin; MacKinnon); 3) A liberal-plural understanding of sexuality, or: ‘sex positivity’ (Rubin; Willis). I argue for a new Marxist approach in which sexuality is understood as both shaped by and exceeding its capitalist form: sexual desire is always mediated – there is no natural, ‘true’ sexuality beneath its capitalist form – but at the same time it exceeds its capitalist form: it is not solely defined by domination. We should neither celebrate sexuality as an already liberated sphere, nor de-politicize it, nor condemn sexuality as inherently oppressive. The question is not how to ‘liberate’ sexuality as such, but how to transform the social forms that organize desire – such that sexual relations might become thinkable beyond capitalist domination, reification, and commodification.

talks.title: The Labor Struggle in Dutch Higher Education: An Organizer Roundtable
talks.abstract:
This roundtable brings together activists and organizers from five different Dutch universities to share experiences from the labor struggle in higher education. After last year's historic strikes, what are the current challenges and opportunities for building solidarity within the academic community and with the (Dutch) working class as a whole?

The panel consists of the following speakers: 

Sam Hamer (UvA) is an active FNV member and is also involved in the action committees UvA Staff for Palestine, UvA voor Vrede, and Casual UvA (for permanent contracts). He will share his experiences of workplace organizing, with a particular focus on organizing around unpopular demands. How to engage colleagues who do not (yet) support your cause? How can activist groups position themselves in relation to the union?

Caitlin Ryan (RUG) is an organizer in OrganizetheRUG. Four years of worker-to-worker organizing in OtR enabled RUG employees to self-organize the program of their relay strike on the faculty level. Caitlin will talk about a question she ran into while mobilizing her coworkers for the strike: do academics see themselves as workers? Asking this helps us to think about why it can be hard to mobilize them around labor issues. 

Willemien Sanders (UU) has been a member of WOinActie from the early days. She will discuss the history of this grassroots movement, its organization and current issues it is working on, as well as some of the challenges it is facing as a flat, non-hierarchical band of committed university employees.

Lotje Siffels (RU) is an organizer in 0.7 and active with Vakbond Solidair met Palestina (VSMP). 0.7 is an activist antifascist network fighting precarity and far-right politics in universities. VSMP is a collective of trade union members committed to justice and international solidarity. 0.7 adapted to different action forms according to what was necessary in the moment, organizing protests, institutional support, involvement in the unions, and advocating for other activist groups. Lotje will talk about the need for solidarity with marginalized employees and democratization in universities.

Arnout van Ree and Cristiana Strava (LEI) will speak about workplace organizing based on their experiences as FNV union organizers. They will share successes, challenges, and lessons from organizing and mobilizing colleagues around issues affecting both the university and wider society. They will reflect on successful strategies, the role of the labor movement, and the relationship between activism and organizing.

talks.title: Beyond the Iron Curtain: Soviet Debates on the Transition to Capitalism and the Brenner Thesis
talks.abstract:
This paper, cowritten with Nicolas Brisset, revisits Robert Brenner’s influential thesis on the transition from feudalism to capitalism by placing it in dialogue with a largely overlooked body of historiography: Soviet debates on feudalism and its transformation. While Western discussions and most notably the Dobb–Sweezy controversy have structured the reception of Brenner’s work, Soviet contributions have remained marginal in accounts of this debate despite addressing closely related questions.

Drawing on Soviet historiography, we reconstruct an alternative intellectual context in which the transition problem was framed not as a stylized passage from feudalism to capitalism, but as a problem of historical periodization grounded in empirical investigations of specific social formations. Soviet historians focused on identifying the “fundamental economic law of feudalism” and on articulating the internal dynamics of feudal social relations, particularly in the Russian case. This perspective contrasts with interpretations emphasizing exogenous drivers such as trade expansion or bourgeois agency.

We show that these debates, although couched in a distinct conceptual vocabulary, converge with core concerns of Brenner’s approach – namely, the primacy of social-property relations and class structures in explaining divergent developmental trajectories. At the same time, Soviet discussions complicate Brenner’s framework by foregrounding the diversity of feudal formations and the methodological challenges of deriving general laws from historically specific cases.

By bringing Soviet historiography into the conversation, the paper contributes to a broader re-evaluation of Marxist debates on the transition. It suggests that the Brenner thesis can be better understood, and potentially reformulated, when read not only against Western Marxist traditions but also in light of intellectual developments that unfolded “on the other side of the Iron Curtain.”

talks.title: The Real Abstraction of Nature: A Wertkritik Critique of the Metabolic Rift
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract:
In the _Grundrisse_, Marx defines capitalism as a social system in which ‘individuals are now ruled by abstractions…’ Abstractions are thus an operative force caught up in social relations and are, according to Alberto Toscano, of an ontological character (Toscano 2008). My paper examines the theoretical implications of the ontological character of these ‘real abstractions’, following Alfred Sohn-Rethel's conceptualisation, for the ‘metabolic rift’ school of eco-Marxism. Does this undo the dualism between nature and labour, in which, as Kohei Saito argues, the former is the substratum of—in other words, _distinct_ from— the latter, when both the categories of ‘nature’ and ‘labour’ are historically specific real abstractions mediated by commodity form and immanent to the logic of capital accumulation?
	 Indeed, Antonia Majaca argues that whilst metabolic rift theory correctly identifies capitalism as the driver of ecological disruption, it nevertheless presupposes a universal, pre-given metabolic relation between the Human and the Natural that capital can unsettle in the first place (Majaca 2025). In this light, despite the rather antagonistic relation between Bruno Latour and Marxist scholars, I argue with Latour that for critique _not to run out of steam_, critical theory ought to examine how the ‘matters of fact’ determined by the relations of production emerge from the ‘matters of concern’ in which both ‘the human’ and the ‘non-human’ participate (Latour 2004). An ecological Marxism, I contend, should therefore address the _plurality_ of ways in which structures and ideology may engage, in Donna Haraway’s formulation, ‘all beings who work and play’ (Haraway 2008) to participate in the reproduction of labour, society, nature, and life. 
In the final analysis, if we understand ideology in the Althusserian sense as a positive absence, experienced only through the _traces_ and _effects_ on labouring bodies, we must then recognise non-human labour as an important locus for theorising—as a place where abstractions materialise. Borrowing from Jason W. Moore’s ‘World-Ecology’ approach, I demonstrate how non-human labour does not merely contribute to the accumulation of capital but also to the reification of ‘value’ and other abstract categories of political economy as such. Overcoming the Society/Nature binary is thus an important step in dismantling the _real_ and _violent_ forms of capitalist abstractions that dominate bodies, reify consciousnesses, and proliferate climate crises and ecological catastrophes in the Capitalocene.

talks.title: Latin America between reaction and rebellion: the far right, US imperialism, and the left
talks.abstract:
The first quarter of the twenty-first century closes with Latin America once again at the centre of global reaction. A new far right has come to power across the region, from Milei in Argentina to Kast in Chile and Paz in Bolivia, while US imperialism has returned to open intervention: in January 2026 the Trump administration captured President Maduro in a military raid on Caracas and announced it would “run” Venezuela, with Cuba and Nicaragua named as the next targets. The decades-long blockade of Cuba tightens further. Yet this offensive is far from uncontested, from student mobilizations in Chile to mass protests across the region. In Bolivia, a popular rebellion of miners, teachers, Indigenous communities, and workers has brought the country to a standstill against the austerity measures of a new right-wing government. In Argentina, Milei’s project confronts sustained resistance in the streets and a renewed Ni Una Menos movement, while the experience of the Frente de Izquierda y de los Trabajadores–Unidad (FIT-U) demonstrates that a revolutionary left can remain organized, and electorally relevant without surrendering to nationalism.
 
This panel analyses the regional conjuncture, understanding that it is a decisive testing ground for the contemporary tasks of the left: how to confront a resurgent far right, how to resist imperialist aggression without falling into the trap of “lesser-evilism” or pseudo-radical campism, and how to build forms of class politics adequate to the present. Bringing together perspectives on Argentina, Cuba, and the broader regional situation, the panel aims to bring Latin American struggles into dialogue with Marxist debates in the Netherlands.

talks.title: Marx after Eurocentrism
talks.abstract: Marx emerged from a thoroughly Eurocentric context, even being called one of the last ‘schoolmen’, steeped in Latin-based scholarly culture. We can see this in his doctoral dissertation, investigating the trajectory of Greek philosophy. Yet it is precisely from within this context that Marx developed an approach to history that negates the kind of Eurocentrism inherent in Hegel’s history of philosophy and philosophy of history. In this paper, I will explore the specifics of this, focusing on the impact of Marx’s interpretation of the Epicurean clinamen or swerve and its afterlife in his methodological reflections on the mode of production. Arguably, it was this perspective that allowed Marx’s ideas to be applied beyond the strictures of the European historical context from which they emerged.

talks.title: Marxist ground rent and the metabolic rift
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract:
"[T]he rent question is returning with a vengeance" (Andreucci 2017, 29). Analyses of a turn of capitalism towards a new stage, rentier capitalism, abound as the influence of traditional capitalist endeavours seems to shrink in relation to rent-extracting digital or financial operations. But in these analyses, the Marxist conception of rent, ground rent, is often neglected or unduly extended (Saito 2025, 2). Similarly, a connection of rent to the recent  rediscovery of Marxism's ecological side remains underexplored (Ehara 2023 , 120). 
In my research, I aim to analyse the dynamics of Marx's classical theory of ground rent as a contributing factor to the metabolic rift under capitalism.
The Marxist theory of ground rent "remains one of the least explored areas in Marxian economics, and few scholars have attempted to apply Marx's concept of rent to the contemporary rentier economy" (Saito 2025, 5). Similarly, "[w]hile some recent eco-Marxists pay attention to Marx's rent theory […] they cannot be considered as an established economic theory of rent." (Ehara 2023, 120). There is therefore an urgent need to establish the direct connection between Marxist rent theory and eco-Marxist theory, not just through a superficial analysis of similarities, but in a manner, which captures the distinct mechanism of rent in the capitalist mode of production and its relation to the rapidly worsening ecological crisis (Otero 2026, 1-2). 
To address this gap, it is necessary to reconstruct the Marxist theory of rent in its connection to Marx's whole political economy, so that a selective, disintegrated application of this theory becomes impossible (see Christophers 2020, xxiv). On the basis of this reconstruction, the relation of rent to nature and the possibility of the expansion of the Marxist theory of ground rent to fit the rentier capitalism framework can be elucidated (Saito 2025, 7; Christophers 2020, xxii; Andreucci 2017, 29-30). To fight the ecological crisis, to analyse class and climate, the eco-Marxist view has to grasp all three classes, bourgeoisie, proletariat, and landlords, and their relation to each other. 
The practical potential of this research is the connection of movements against the excesses of rentierism with movements against environmental destruction, if possible, on a Marxist basis.

talks.title: Salvage Historiography: Walter Benjamin and the Task of the Historian
talks.abstract:
In this paper, I put forward an interpretation of Walter Benjamin’s philosophy of history as ‘salvage historiography.’ 

First, I analyze Benjamin’s critique of nineteenth-century Rankean historicism, which viewed history as coherent and linear-progressive whole that could be known objectively. Benjamin counters this historicism as bourgeois narrativizing that vindicates the existing social order and fetishistically treats history as a commodity object.

Then, I argue with Benjamin against teleological progress-narratives that obfuscate the “catastrophe in permanence” that is taking place. Eschewing the trap of seeking a return to a mythical past instead, Benjamin focuses on rupture, contingency, and discontinuity, proposing a historical materialism in which the “repressed heterogeneity” of the past is liberated.

Following from this, I discuss what I take to be the task of the historian that Benjamin presents, namely to rescue historical objects from conformist history-writing. The present is not viewed as the overcoming of past history, instead the oppressed of the past make their claim on our present. This amounts to an active historiography that doesn’t concern itself with linearity but with the constant repurposing of history for political struggle in the present, searching for the “productive polarity” of “the historical and the political,” evaluating the historical object on its insurgent capabilities. The historian can construct a dialectical image in which the historical object forms an explosive relationship with the present, a “secret agreement” which is the collision of different temporal modalities. This opens up the historical object and allows it to emerge out of habitual historical thinking so as to speak to us differently.

Finally, I introduce the concept of ‘salvage historiography’ as encapsulating the task of the historian, which I identify with the Benjaminian figure of the ragpicker. I understand this historiographical approach of rescuing the waste, the debris, and trying to fashion something out of it, as contributing to a project of salvage communism – part of Benjamin’s ‘organized pessimism.’ This organized pessimism realizes recognizes that “the ‘state of emergency’ in which we live is not the exception but the rule.” I focus on Palestine, where the still-ongoing Nakba makes this permanent catastrophe particularly clear. The task of the historian becomes organizing pessimism and salvaging the messianic impulses from the ruins of catastrophe, preparing a revolution that understands itself to be always-already too late, as obligation to the downtrodden and slain masses of the past.

talks.title: Capitalism and the Generational Rift: Towards a Gen Z Socialism
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract:
Marxist theorists have long shunned generational theory, arguing that it serves to obscure other more fundamental aspects of the political economy, such as class and market rule. At the same time, it appears that the current crisis of capitalism is experienced by many young people across the world in distinctly generational terms. Recent years have seen a wave of ‘Gen Z’ protests in countries across the Global South, including Indonesia, Nepal, the Philippines, Kenya, Madagascar and Morocco, often led by lose collectives that explicitly identify as generational subjects, such as ‘Gen Z Mada’ in Madagascar, or ‘GenZ 212’ in Morocco. 
This paper builds on previous work (presented at HM 2025) to argue that both form and political content of the Gen Z protest wave are shaped by the effects of a persistent global accumulation crisis and the associated resurgence of rentierism, state capitalism and imperialist warfare. Notably, many Gen Z mobilizations also address metabolic concerns such as climate adaptation, water, electricity, health, mining, which are likewise shaped by the dynamics of capital.
The standard references in bourgeois generational theory, Karl Mannheim’s 1928 Problem of Generations, as well as the work of William Strauss and Neil Howe, fail to make sense of capitalism’s central role in shaping the generational experience. I develop the notion of a ‘generational rift’ as an alternative framework to discuss the problem of generations from a Marxist perspective. Drawing on recently published work by Timothy Mitchell (2026), I argue that the generational rift points to the temporal dimension of capitalism’s metabolic rift, leading succeeding generations to repay the costs of present extractions. The target of generational hatred should, thus, not be the boomer, but rather the nepo baby – and by extension capitalism itself: the system the structurally produces futurelessness as a generational condition.

talks.title: Materialist Epistemology and Polarization. Strategies for a Militant Epistemology
talks.abstract:
The contemporary political landscape is characterized by polarizing phenomena: political leaders continuously identify an enemy, reinforce the unquestionable validity of their own positions at the expense of others, and emphasize the value of a specific exclusionary identity configuration (e.g. white-male-heterosexual-Christian), thereby identifying the other as an invalid interlocutor. Faced with growing social polarization, epistemology has not ignored the phenomenon and has found in Marxism a valid theoretical instrument.
The paper will be divided as follows: (A) an epistemological-social diagnosis and (B) an epistemological-political construction.
A) Presentation of the phenomenon of polarization and description of its socio-political characteristics through a reconstruction of the epistemic configurations useful for a theoretical anatomy of polarization. The theoretical reference is Hinge Epistemology: the model that recognizes the existence of pre-reflective hinge commitments which make possible both a shared access to the world and the very exercise of epistemic justification. This theoretical model allows the identification of the two forms of disagreement that sustain the possibility of polarization: deep disagreement and peer disagreement.
B) Presentation of Marxism as a theoretical instrument capable of constructing a bridge between socio-economic and cultural conditions. The possible solutions through the materialist framework are:
1.	The theory of hegemony through Gramsci: it is possible to consider the concept of hegemony as an instrument capable of overcoming the distinction between theory and praxis, allowing the identification of the centers of reproduction of superstructures — and therefore also of epistemic hinges — in order to rearticulate them (thus triggering a process of reproduction of a non-polarizing or differently polarizing superstructure); 
2.	The construction of a sociological model capable of identifying the common background shared by polarized entities in order to neutralize polarization. This becomes possible thanks to the theoretical instruments developed by Marxism: the relation between social interests and classes; the measurement of capitalist oppression and its relation to the alienation of labor; the relation between culture and economic structure. These are all instruments capable of understanding who polarized entities really are and what they have in common, thereby constructing a neutral ground upon which confrontation becomes possible. 
Today, polarization is not only a social phenomenon but also a political strategy aimed at perpetuating the reproduction of asymmetrical power relations. It is time for epistemology too to participate in the struggle. through its own instruments and within its own terrains.
