talks.title: Scenes from a shotgun marriage: the history and future of Freudo-marxism
talks.abstract:
Since its very beginning, Marxism has had a both necessary and strained relationship with (social) psychology. Marx himself, in the 1844 manuscripts as well as in the ‘fetishism’ chapter of Capital, drew on psychology to make sense of capitalism. Reversely, the emergence of psychology, particularly psychoanalysis, in the early 20th century, was soon followed by attempts (e.g. by Erich Fromm and Herbert Marcuse) to bring this new science in dialogue with Marxism in order to, on the one hand, explain psychic suffering and pathologies through the ills of the capitalist system, and, on the other hand, make sense of our psychic attachment to and/or libidinal investment in capitalism or fascism.
        	Historically, there have been some pivotal moments during which attempts were made to synthesize Marxism and psychoanalysis, for instance in the 1930s (e.g. by Reich and the Frankfurt School, to analyze the rise of fascism) and in the 1960s (e.g. by Lacan, Marcuse and Debord, to make sense of the emerging consumer society). Just as often, there have been critiques of such attempts, for instance by Deleuze & Guattari and Foucault, or by analytical or antihumanist Marxists.
        	Recently, there seems to have been a resurgence in the cross-fertilization of psychoanalysis and Marxism, for instance in the work of scholars such as Todd McGowan, Alberto Toscano, and Amy Allen. The rise of far-right populism and neofascism in particular, which so clearly goes against the immediate self-interest of the masses, makes clear that irrational forces are at play that cannot be sufficiently explained or understood through a purely materialist, Marxist analysis.
        	In this panel for the Marxism NL conference, we, a group of philosophers from different universities and different backgrounds who share an interest in ‘freudo-marxism’, want to thematize this cross-fertilization of Marxism and psychoanalysis. What does psychoanalysis bring to the table that Marxism on its own cannot do or understand (and vice versa)? How can it help us to make sense of (neo)fascism, but also: of consumer culture and the continuing allure of capitalism for so many people, or of gender and race relations, etc.? And what are potential advantages and pitfalls of this confrontation, and how have different thinkers, from the Frankfurt School to today, dealt with them?

talks.title: Exploitation-based social class and political participation
talks.abstract:
Departing from recent discussions about social class, we develop hypotheses based on the idea of the power antagonism between the workers and capitalists, and the implications of this antagonism for political participation. While the mainstream sociological occupation- and income-based schemes can measure social mobility within the existing economic conditions, social class based on exploitation is more relevant for measuring political empowerment. We adopt a quantitative empirical approach to analyse the class structure, class consciousness, and their effects on political behaviour.    
We recreate E.O. Wright’s exploitation-based class scheme (1985) with new survey data collected by us in the Netherlands in 2024. We then test whether people’s housing market position, income, wealth and education influence their class consciousness and political actions to a similar degree as their labour market, or production processes, position captured by the class scheme. Exploitation-based social class, more than income, wealth, housing, or occupation, predicts class consciousness and shapes patterns of political participation in the Netherlands; though education remains the strongest driver of direct political action and voting. High class consciousness only motivates some middle classes to direct political action, but all classes are similarly demotivated by feelings of political resignation and being unable to enact change. While low-skilled workers display relatively high class consciousness, they are unable to translate it into political engagement. Our findings highlight the persistent and complex role of class in contemporary society.

talks.title: Imperialism and the Dutch far right
talks.abstract: The rising far right has a complex and varying relationship to the imperialism of different national bourgeoisies and states, and particularly in the Netherlands. In general, the ascension of the far right is linked to a turn away from the ‘hyperglobalization’ of the period of the most intense neoliberalism in the late 1990s and the beginning of the 21st century, towards a somewhat more nationalist form of capitalism, less dominated by the biggest multinational corporations and banks. Brexit in the UK and Trump’s ‘America First’ in the US are examples. The extent of far-right nationalism is however constrained by the room available to fractions of a specific national bourgeoisie. In the Netherlands, the biggest far-right party, Geert Wilders’ Freedom Party (PVV), in keeping with an overall ‘postfascist’ course based on compromise with the country’s very multinationally-oriented capital, has taken some distance from fantasies about ‘Nexit’. The smaller Forum for Democracy (FvD) continues however to flirt with a more improbable, ideologically extreme international orientation. This paper will explore the class basis and (geo)political implications of these different courses.

talks.title: Contingency, Class Struggle, and Challenging Unfree Labor in Antebellum California: A Case for Historical Materialism
talks.abstract: This presentation defends historical materialism as essential for understanding and pursuing social change, without reducing history to deterministic laws. Drawing on political Marxism, especially the work of Charles Post and Ellen Meiksins Wood, it argues that historical transformation emerges from contingent class struggles shaped by specific social property relations. The conflict between slaveholders and northern capitalists over the American West made antebellum California a crucial site in this struggle. Reinterpreting Stacey L. Smith’s work on unfree labor through a Marxist lens, the presentation examines how Black Californians navigated overlapping regimes of slavery, wage labor, and dependency, compounded by legal exclusion. Their position reveals how class struggle developed across multiple forms of coercion and how resistance emerged within unstable and contradictory labor regimes. Rather than offering a deterministic model of social transformation, the paper argues that historical materialism helps identify the structural constraints, openings, and experiments through which emancipatory politics become possible. In this sense, the struggles of unfree laborers in antebellum California offer concrete historical lessons for contemporary movements confronting today’s stratified and precarious workforce.

talks.title: On the Crossroads to Freedom: Lusophone African Revolutionary Diplomacy against Colonialism and Apartheid
talks.abstract:
The revolutionary diplomacy of Portuguese speaking (Lusophone) African liberation movements during the 1960s and 1970s was central to their struggle against Portuguese colonialism. This transcended traditional state-centric models of diplomacy, emphasizing solidarity and grassroots internationalism. A pivotal moment in this diplomatic approach was the UN-OAU Conference on Southern Africa held in Oslo in 1973, where liberation movements from Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau and Cabo Verde, and other Southern African territories met with state and non-state actors to address their struggles on the global stage. Conferences were not just venues for political discourse but strategic platforms for the articulation of anti-colonial struggles and the mobilization of international solidarity. 

For Lusophone African liberation movements, the Oslo Conference represented an opportunity to present their cases and gain recognition in the international community, bypassing some of the diplomatic privileges of recognized states. The Oslo conference, in particular, embodied this unique form of revolutionary diplomacy, where liberation movements became legitimized partners for diplomatic engagement with Southern Africa. This form of diplomacy allowed the movements to build networks of support, challenge colonialism and apartheid by conceptualising boycott, divestment and sanctions campaigns, and frame their liberation struggles within broader global narratives of justice, anticolonialism and emancipation. As such, the Oslo conference played a crucial role in the success of Lusophone African liberation efforts.

talks.title: What’s in a class? A political philosophical analysis of the precariat
talks.abstract:
We are back in a world of class. But how do we make sense of it? In addition to more mainstream sociological accounts that emerged in the aftermath of the 2008 crisis, Marxists have since then attempted to update Marx’s comprehensive political class analyses for the current political moment (Blumenfeld 2025, Chibber 2022, Cicherchia 2019, Winant 2024).
My paper aims to contribute to the debate about the contemporary class structure and its political-theoretical consequences by integrating insights from the ‘precariat’-debate. I will examine to what extent we can think about the precariat (introduced by Standing 2014) as its own class of workers. I will argue that on the grounds of three political-philosophical concepts, it is impossible to clearly separate precarious workers from all other workers: (a) the worker-precarious worker relationship cannot accurately be described as exploitative, (b) while sometimes a regularly employed person might arbitrarily interfere with a precarious worker’s freedom, there is no structural reason to speak of intra-worker class domination, and (c) there is no structural difference in two out of three levels of ‘material interests’.
From this discussion, I will argue, Marxists can learn two things about classes: (a) that working class formation is a dynamic process (Mayer-Ahuja 2025, Thompson 1966) and (b) that even a focus on material interests (Chibber 2022, Wright 2005) needs to include a dynamic element. This creates possibilities to unite workers against the structural domination they face on the labour market.

talks.title: Imperialism at Work: Rescue and Innocence in Africa
talks.abstract:
This paper examines fascism, imperialism, and colonialism through two contemporary African stories: Libya after Gaddafi, and South Africa in the age of Trump’s “white refugee” politics. Libya reveals the logic of imperialist intervention. The fall of Gaddafi (important is to exam what Geddafi represented for imperialist eyes) did not end domination; it reorganised it. South Africa offers a different but connected story. Here, fascistic politics appears through an ideological inversion: white as victims of racial persecution. Trump’s defence of white South Africans as refugees transforms colonial narrative into reactionary ideology of threat to civilisation. What is civilisation today?

Taken together, Libya and South Africa reveal two fronts of one imperialist contradiction. In Libya, imperialism destroys in the name of rescue. In South Africa, imperialism falsifies history in the name of innocence (victimhood). One works through material violence, the other through ideological reversal. Both show how the logic of global domination works. A Marxist analysis must expose this disguise and return history to the struggles of the oppressed.

talks.title: Capital accumulation through labour infrastructures: Rethinking precarious wage work as  the uneven circulation of labour power
talks.abstract:
Over the last decades, wage work guarantees less and less the social reproduction of labour. The erosion of the living wage, “a wage level… that is sufficient to afford a decent standard of living for workers and their families” (ILO, 2024), has been mainly explained as a process of precarization. Precarization refers to wage work shifting away from the so-called ‘standard employment relation’ (SER) – full time, open employment with a single employer providing stable wage and benefits – towards temporary, part-time, outsourced work, self-employment and gig work.  
While informative, a precarization lens cannot account for the fundamental change wage work is undergoing under contemporary capitalism. Such a lens underplays the structural role of state coercion and violence (e.g., through welfare conditionality, activation policies, migration legislation, carceral policies) in enforcing racialized, gendered and ableist labour-capital relations. Second, by focusing on individuals’ work and employment conditions, it does not address how labour gets socially reproduced in the absence of a living wage. Last, it holds onto an understanding of labour as a ‘stock’ of workers tied to a specific workplace, albeit for less time, despite the growing evidence that capital increasingly sources labour temporarily, as a ‘flow,’ turning it into surplus population. 
In this paper, we develop a Marxist infrastructural approach to reconceptualize contemporary wage work as uneven circulations of labour power. To do so, we combine insights from scholarship on the logistic revolution, which has its roots in the work of Marx, Rosa Luxemburg and David Harvey, with insights from Black and decolonial Marxism, social reproduction theory and critical border theory. 
A Marxist infrastructural approach shifts the analysis from the employment contract to the infrastructural conditions making certain labour forces available to capital only when they are needed and under specific, heterogeneous conditions. It unveils the role of multiple actors, legislation and public policies in unevenly modulating the circulation of labour power – by combining specific forms of coercion – along, among other, migrant, racial-ethnic, gender, disability lines. Last, it foregrounds how capital accumulation relies on value originating outside capitalist production for its own reproduction.
This theoretical approach allows to reconceptualize resistance occurring in multiple locations of the infrastructure of labour power circulation, leading to an expansive understanding of class struggle beyond the point of production. 
In the coming two years, this conceptual approach will be deployed to empirically analyse circulations of labour power through warehouses across Europe.
