talks.title: Marxism and geography
talks.abstract:
Marxism and geography
Marxism played an important role in human geography, especially in what became ‘critical human geography’. Marxist geography emerged in response to positivist tendencies in the discipline that glossed over the political and classed nature of spatial developments. Building on Marxist theory and geographic-historical materialism, Marxist geographers engage issues of uneven development, the metabolic relation to nature, the production of (urban) space, and geographic variations in capital’s social formations. While influential, the influence of Marxism in geography has subsided over the last few decades.
This roundtable brings together scholars who use Marxism to study space and place of, in, or from the Netherlands. It celebrates and hopes to reinvigorate Marxism in (Dutch) human geography. The following speakers will provide brief presentations and discuss the present and future of Marxist geography in the Netherlands:
    • Reijer Hendrikse: financialisation
    • Sander van Lanen: social infrastructure and social reproduction
    • Maithe van Lith: international relations
    • Jaap Nieuwenhuis: local and class identities – the role of volunteering
    • Erik Swyngedouw: climate change and political-ecology
    • Agata Troost: repoliticising neighbourhood effects

talks.title: The Dutch Marxists – an introduction
talks.abstract: If the Dutch Marxists of the early 1900s are known today, it is largely because some of them are remembered as ultraleft radicals criticised by Lenin in Left-Wing Communism. Two of them are also known as innovative poets. The purpose of this book, a relatively small selection from many hundreds of articles, is to show that there is more to Dutch Marxism than anti-parliamentarism or a lost battle with Lenin. Several Dutch Marxists played a role in debates in the Second International, especially on the role of the general strike and on anti-militarism. Dutch Marxists wrote on a wide range of subjects, including art, religion, culture, social and political questions, strategy and tactics, and economic theory and policy. Politically, some contributions are widely known, but their work on economics, especially on the Marxist theory of crises, imperialism and long waves, is less well known outside a limited group of specialists. Even in the Netherlands, very few realise that the non-Marxist pioneer of econometrics Jan Tinbergen paid tribute to his Marxist teachers. The work by Dutch Marxists in the early years of the twentieth century produced new insights into the development of capitalism by pioneering the concept of long waves.

talks.title: Technofeudalism and Contemporary Literature
talks.abstract:
This panel addresses the recent debate in Marxist theory about whether capitalism is in the process of
being significantly altered, or even superseded, by a new social order or mode of production to which
a number of scholars have given the name “technofeudalism.” Each paper examines this debate and its
key concept with reference to literary texts published in recent years that address key technofeudal
themes. The panel also considers the role played by culture in general, and literature in particular, in
the technofeudal character and project of our present.

**Adam Kelly (University College Dublin)
The Novel in Technofeudal Times: Eleanor Catton’s Birnam Wood (2023)**

This paper begins by offering an overview of the technofeudalism debates among Marxists, referencing
work by scholars including Yanis Varoufakis, Cedric Durand, Evgeny Morozov, Jodi Dean, and Matt
Seybold. It outlines the various characteristics of contemporary political economy and culture that have
been designated technofeudal, and considers the arguments of Marxists who have refuted such a
designation. The paper then briefly sketches the classic relationship proposed by Marxist literary
scholars between the rise of capitalism and the rise of the novel, from the early modern period to the
present. This leads to a question: if, as some scholars claim, we are moving from capitalism to
technofeudalism, and if capitalism and the novel are inextricably intertwined, then does this mean we
are moving beyond the novel? The final section of the paper aims to answer this question by turning
to a recent novel, Eleanor Catton’s Birnam Wood. Set in New Zealand, a country that features heavily
in the postapocalyptic dreamscape of the Silicon Valley leadership class, Catton’s novel imagines the
global beginnings of a new social, political, and economic order. The paper argues that Birnam Wood
offers a self-reflexive engagement with what any possible transition from capitalism to
technofeudalism would mean for the representation of class relations and social totality in the novel
form. The paper thus seeks to demonstrate what literature can bring to the debates on technofeudalism
that cannot be articulated in other forms.

**Mathieu Bokestael (University College Dublin)
The Immortal King’s Two Bodies: Testing the Technofeudal Thesis in Vauhini Vara’s The
Immortal King Rao (2022)**

This paper considers the technofeudal thesis – the argument that technological corporations are
increasingly acting as feudal lords and are thereby changing the social order and mode of production
– through a close reading of depictions of political and biomedical immunity in Vauhini Vara's novel
The Immortal King Rao (2022). In this Pulitzer-nominated speculative novel, Rao, a precocious child
from a Dalit background, grows up to become an accomplished tech CEO and the leader of the world-
governing ‘Board of Corporations.’ Upon his death, Rao transfers his memories to his daughter Athena
in a move that seems to echo both contemporary transhumanist thought in Silicon Valley and the feudal
doctrine of the king’s two bodies. Yet, as Athena’s letters, despite the injection of Rao’s memories,
constitute a passionate defense of the necessity of communion in the face of climate catastrophe, and
not an affirmation of her father’s right, the continuity of the king’s immortal ‘body corporate’ is shown
to be incomplete. This paper therefore argues that by satirising Rao’s attempts at achieving biological
immunity/immortality, the novel critiques a return towards the kind of social order in which the
sovereign had total political and legal immunity. The novel registers how what critics have called
technofeudalism also constitutes an attempt to regain, for the now corporate lords, the feudal
sovereign’s absolute immunity. Yet while The Immortal King Rao bears a few similarities to Aravind
Adiga’s The White Tiger (2008) in its epistolary nature, (partial) Indian setting, and critique of
contemporary techno-capitalism, it is also written by a well-known reporter for notoriously liberal
magazines such as The Atlantic, The New Yorker, The New York Times, or even The Wall Street
Journal. The question thus becomes whether this critique of what one may call technofeudalism does
not serve to relieve the capitalist system from responsibility for the harms of contemporary techno-
oligarchy. In other words, what does the novel satirise and critique: is it the capitalist system as such,
or is it a form of capitalism that is starting to resemble feudalism too much? By investigating this
question, the paper will ask whether there is a risk, for Marxists, in adopting the language of
technofeudalism.

**Rhona Jamieson (University College Dublin)
The Neoreactionary Text: The Meeting of Technofeudalism and Accelerationism**

While originating on the left, the term ‘technofeudalism’ gained prominence in the US after it was
used by Steve Bannon in a January 2025 interview attacking Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk.
Technofeudalism therefore entered the mainstream in a manner that highlighted a fracture within the
American Right’s coalition. How did the technological monopolies of Silicon Valley relate to the
MAGA project, its nativist grievance politics and nostalgia for traditional manufacturing? This paper
analyses this point of fracture within the right-wing ecosystem by focusing on Neoreaction, a
movement that has both critiqued and championed a social system comparable to technofeudalism. By
analysing original fiction and essays produced by neoreactionaries, the paper explores the relationship
between Curtis Yarvin’s feudal vision of the ‘sovcorps’ and Nick Land’s technological accelerationism
(originally derived from Marxist theory). Short stories such as Zero HP Lovecraft’s ‘The Gig
Economy’ (2022) draw upon the legacy of 1990s accelerationism to depict data-harvesting platforms
as parasitic Lovecraftian entities. Cloud-serfdom as a form of entrapped passivity is depicted in styles
that draw upon the cybergothic writings of the 1990s. The paper then goes on to consider the content
of neoreactionary literature in relation to the aristocratic mode of cultural production practiced by
Passage Press, a recently established right-wing press based in California. Passage’s close relationship
to neoreactionary writers, and emphasis on printing hard-copy editions of blogs by Yarvin and Land,
signals both a championing of the neoreactionary project and an opposition to what Matt Seybold has
dubbed the ‘technofeudal text.’ Passage’s return to print, while at odds with any model of technological
accelerationism, is nevertheless rooted in an aristocratic model of cultural production in which the
print text is a marker of prestige and entry into a cognitive elite. This paper proposes a strategy of
reading the ‘neoreactionary text’ in order to map the contradictions of the contemporary Tech Right.

talks.title: Indonesia free from Holland – now?  Dutch Communists and Indonesian independence
talks.abstract:
Anti-colonialism was one of the lines of division between the reformist and revolutionary left in early twentieth century Netherlands. In 1914 the SDP introduced the slogan ‘Indië los van Holland’ to express its support for Indonesian independence. Until the mid-thirties, this slogan was used by the Communist Party before being abandoned. For over a decade the Communist Party instead supported the formation of a Dutch-Indonesian commonwealth before shifting course again and taking up the old demand in 1948. The commonwealth policy, the Dutch Communists now declared, had been a serious error. Their Indonesian comrades went as far as criticizing it as ‘reformism’ that had ‘seriously endangered the Indonesian national revolution’. 
Both abandoning the demand for Indonesian independence and the reversal to the old slogan in 1948 have often been interpreted as resulting from directives coming from Moscow and the shift from the popular front strategy to the Cold War politics of the ‘two camps’. CPN-documents from the late forties show that the Dutch Communist leadership’s reasoning was based on geopolitical calculations. In the immediate post-1945 years, Indonesian independence was considered to benefit British and then US imperialism. When the party reverted to the demand for Indonesian independence, the old slogan had come to mean an Indonesia ruled by the Communist Party. The paradoxical outcome was that in 1949, after the repression of the Indonesian Communists, the Dutch Communists voted against the transfer of sovereignty to the new Indonesian state. Rather than simply originating from Soviet directives, the shifts in Communist policy regarding Indonesian independence were linked to changing prospects for the Communists parties in both Indonesia and the Netherlands.

talks.title: Protectionisme onder de vooruitstrevende burgerij (1873 tot en met 1896): Henry George en de Bond voor Landnationalisatie
talks.abstract:
Tegen de achtergrond van de Grote Depressie van 1873 tot en met 1896 namen een aantal vooraanstaande Nederlandse ondernemers het op voor protectionisme in de vorm van landnationalisatie, gereguleerde graanprijzen en werkverschaffing voor de ontginning van ‘woeste gronden’. Om gehoor te geven aan deze eisen werd een politieke partij genaamd de Bond voor Landnationalisatie opgericht. Hoewel deze ondernemers heren bleven van zowel productiemiddelen als ‘werkvolk’, worden zij door latere historici gekenschetst als socialisten. Is dit een terechte karakterisering? 

In de negentiende eeuw kwam het in Nederland voor dat ondernemers zich opwierpen als leidende figuren in de arbeidersbeweging. Jan Stoffel, Daniël de Clercq, Derk Roelfs Mansholt en Vitus Bruinsma waren ondernemers die veelal hun verdiensten trokken uit vormen van bedrijfsvoering die afweken van traditioneel kapitalisme, maar zeker niet onder de categorie ‘loonarbeid’ kunnen vallen. Stoffel was een houtfabrikant, De Clercq leidinggevende in een coöperatief adviesbureau, Mansholt (heren)boer en Bruinsma naast schrijver van boekjes over kwakzalverij ook oprichter van de Vereniging tegen de Kwakzalverij. Binnen de bredere Nederlandse kiesrechtbeweging zochten zij initieel samenwerking met de Sociaal-Democratische Bond van Domela Nieuwenhuis. 

De politieke inspiratiebronnen, artikelen en polemieken van deze ondernemers verhullen dat zij een eigenzinnige interpretatie van het socialisme volgden, die verklaard kan worden vanuit de klassepositie. In tegenstelling tot sommige socialisten en alle communisten die opriepen voor de gedwongen afschaffing van het kapitalistische staatsapparaat en al het privaatbezit (waaronder de grond, productiemiddelen en sociale klassenverhoudingen), richtten deze mannen zich hoofdzakelijk op de wettige beperking van privaat grondbezit. Hiervoor werd door de bovengenoemde heren in 1889 de Bond voor Landnationalisatie opgericht. Zij werden door filosoof Henry George en zijn 'single tax' voorzien van theorie. 

De ondernemers erkenden de sociaal ontwrichtende problemen van excessief kapitalisme, maar stonden zeker niet voor een alternatief economisch systeem. Zijn zagen hoofdzakelijk in de speculatieve activiteiten van grootgrondbezitters, en mindere mate financiers, de oorzaak van de sociale kwestie. Het is daarom aannemelijk dat met landnationalisatie het behoud van kapitalisme  hun overkoepelende doel was, samen met een pleidooi voor wetgevende concessies zoals het algemeen kiesrecht, toegankelijk onderwijs, volksgezondheid en lagere huren. Met een reden ontwikkelt de reformistische sociaaldemocratie zich parallel aan deze protectionisten richting een ideologie die het socialisme hoopt te bereiken op vreedzame weg via de stembus.

talks.title: Ontzuiling en haar consequenties
talks.abstract: Ik ga uiteenzetten wat de socio-economische ontwikkelingen waren die de ontzuiling mogelijk hebben gemaakt. Dit lijkt een vaak genoeg besproken onderwerp, maar een marxistische blik op dit fenomeen is vooralsnog uitgebleven. Tevens geeft elk extra verstreken jaar in de een-en-twintigste eeuw ons meer informatie over de gevolgen ervan. Om de ontzuiling te snappen, moet ook kort een analyse gemaakt worden van de Verzuiling. Ik wil betogen dat de Verzuiling, aan het eind van de negentiende eeuw, de reactie was van de burgerlijke samenleving op het aanbreken van de Industriële Revolutie in Nederland. Met de komst van de economische moderniteit in Nederland en de daaruitvloeiende „sociale kwestie” werd de oude burgerlijke samenleving gedreven om te veranderen of te verdwijnen: haar antwoord was Abraham Kuyper en de Verzuiling. Door het tumult van de eerste helft van de twintigste eeuw wist verzuild Nederland zich een weg te banen, soms standvastiger, soms in crisis verkerend. Uiteindelijk ontzuilde Nederland pas rond de vervolmaking van de verzorgingsstaat, eind jaren 1960, begin jaren 1970. Het klassieke narratief zegt ons dat de ontzuiling door nieuwe ontwikkelingen in de communicatiemiddelen komt. Dit is zeker een deel ervan, maar negeert andere grote factoren: de politiek-economische ontwikkelingen, m.n. de deïndustrialisatie van Nederland. Daarnaast zijn het begin van de Europese economische integratie en integratie in de Amerikaanse mondiale productieketens belangrijke ontwikkelingen die diepgaande socio-economische, socio-culturele en politieke gevolgen hadden in Nederlandse samenleving. Met deze socio-economische ontwikkelingen in het achterhoofd probeer ik de belangrijkste politieke ontwikkelingen na de ontzuiling te duiden. Een paar belangrijke voorbeelden die ik ga behandelen zijn de samensmelting van de verschillende christelijke partijen tot het CDA, de opkomst van Pim Fortuyn en de neergang van eerst het CDA en daarna de PvdA. Ter ondersteuning van de politieke analyse zal hier en daar naar culturele ontwikkelingen verwezen worden, bv. de Gabberscène in de jaren 1990, het Hyvestijdperk en de hedendaagse cultuur.

talks.title: “Necessary Surplus”: Mexican Jornaleros under contemporary U.S. politics
talks.track: Social reproduction, care and Marxist feminism
talks.abstract: Mexican _jornaleros_ in the United States sustain essential sectors of the economy, including agriculture, construction, and food systems, while increasingly subjected to criminalization, deportability, labor precarity, and violent anti-migrant enforcement. Under the current authoritarian turn in U.S. politics, migrant workers are simultaneously rendered economically indispensable and politically disposable. This paper argues that contemporary anti-migrant politics in the United States should be understood as a colonial and authoritarian strategy for governing racialized labor through deportability, disposability, and the destabilization of migrant social reproduction. It examines how authoritarian politics increasingly constitute migrant workers as surplus or waste populations whose labor remains economically indispensable while their lives are rendered politically and socially disposable. The paper proposes that Mexican _jornaleros_ occupy a paradoxical position as “necessary surplus”: they are structurally essential to sectors such as agriculture, construction, food systems, and informal labor markets, while simultaneously subjected to criminalization, marginalization, precarity, and violence. Drawing on theories of social reproduction, authoritarianism, and surplus populations, the paper argues that raids, detention, deportation, family separation, workplace terror, and anti-migrant policing operate as forms of violence directed not only at migrants workers themselves, but at the infrastructures that sustain migrant life, including kinship networks, housing, mobility, care, and community formation. The paper further contends that the contemporary criminalization of Mexican _jornaleros_ reflects a fascistizing reorganization of social reproduction under colonial capitalism. Within this configuration, the very conditions that enable migrant survival and collective reproduction become targets of surveillance, punishment, and destruction. By foregrounding the intersection of racialized labor extraction, authoritarian governance, and the policing of social reproduction, the paper seeks to contribute to contemporary debates on colonial capitalism and the authoritarian restructuring of labor and life reproduction.

talks.title: In Search of Universality: The Necessities of Leftist Politics in Times of Crisis
talks.abstract:
Nancy Fraser diagnosed a prevalent distinction in modern-day leftist politics which has contributed to the paralysation of wide liberatory projects. Fraser sees two camps in the modern left, characterised by their privileging of 'redistribution' against 'recognition'.

Recognition politics defines a large section of today's politics; the privileging of difference and the defence of particular identities have decentred universality, and any claim to shared, unifying principles is viewed with wide scepticism. However, this radical fetishisation of particularity disables the possibility of a wider front politics of liberation by refusing to be subsumed into broader movements through strategic alliances. This has led to a situation where the left is fragmented into identitarian conflicts which serve to other people within the same left spectrum. 

On the other side of that, we encounter redistribution, a traditionalist left that stems from a nostalgia for more classical Marxist and Leninist analysis of class as a central category of analysis. While such views have served as a sharp critique of capitalist exploitation, they have often been reductive of difference and become in themselves an abstract universality which fails to grasp the concrete conditions that make a class emerge as such. Moreover, such an analysis relies too much on a transhistorical conception of labour, a form of labour which is fetishised instead of critically deconstructed; such a viewpoint fails to see beyond historically specific forms of organisation that generate the form of labour which it universalises. 

In this talk, I want to initiate a move away from this dichotomy of the contemporary left. By exploring Hegel's concept of the concrete universal, I want to envision how universality can be emergent from concrete conditions without hypostasising itself into a flat metaphysics. The concrete universal can help us deconstruct forms of abstract universality that have come to erase difference, while still retaining a fluid and ever-changing universality that can serve as a ground upon which to fight from. The question remains, what sort of concrete universalities can guide a wider front left politics in our day and age?

talks.title: The last Great Depression and its aftermath
talks.abstract: The world financial crisis starting in 2007/2008 did not end soon as many commentators had it. In fact, it lasted and continued for many years and affected the whole world economy. Accordingly, it is possible to view it as the fourth great depression in the history of modern capitalism. All preceding great depressions ushered in a wave of transformations, changing the structure and form of world capitalism for decennia to come. So, the salient question is:  What are the transformations in world capitalism triggered by this most recent of the Great Depressions? How did and how does capitalism change?

talks.title: Where is reproductive labour in the just energy transition? A feminist analysis of the extraction and manufacturing of energy production in Chile and Sweden
talks.track: Social reproduction, care and Marxist feminism
talks.abstract: This article analyses labour relations in the mining and manufacturing industries that are needed for the energy transition. We draw attention to the often-overlooked reproductive labour that fundamentally underpins energy systems. In doing so, this article makes two key contributions: (1) it proposes an analytical framework for mapping the variegated forms of reproductive labour that sustain the lithium-copper-battery commodity chain from extraction and processing in Antofagasta, Chile to manufacture of lithium-ion batteries in Skellefteå, Sweden, and (2) it offers empirically grounded insights that pays attention to reproductive labour and the persistence of exploitation and calls for a reconceptualization of justice in energy transitions. This paper fills a substantial theoretical and empirical gap by analysing the hidden costs, especially for low-income, unskilled, immigrant workers, who provide reproductive work crucial in sustaining the shift towards the energy transition, yet suffer from social and economic marginalization.

talks.title: The Conceptual Aptness of Strike in Digital Labour Domains: Resistance, Justice, and What’s to Come
talks.abstract:
This paper examines the conceptual aptness of the notion of strike within so called click-work contexts. Drawing on insights from Global Labour History, the paper first reconstructs a baseline understanding of strike as a collective, coordinated withdrawal of labour aimed at exerting economic or political pressure. It distinguishes strikes from smaller-scale, everyday forms of resistance by emphasising collective identity, coordination, and the disruption of production. The analysis then engages four major theoretical traditions – liberal, republican, Marxist, and feminist – to develop a more theoretical and normatively grounded account of strike. Despite important differences, these traditions converge on key features: the withdrawal of labour, the formation of collective identity, and the contestation of power asymmetries.
Building on this conceptual framework, the paper turns to digital labour platforms and investigates existing forms of resistance among platform workers. While delivery workers have demonstrated the capacity to engage in recognisable strike actions, click-workers characterised by extreme dispersion, anonymity, and algorithmic management face structural barriers to collective organisation and coordinated work stoppage. Empirical examples suggest that their resistance tends to take fragmented, often individualised forms that do not neatly fit traditional conceptions of strike.
In response, the paper argues for a reconceptualisation of strike that foregrounds its performative and future-oriented dimensions rather than its strictly material and organisational features. By shifting the analytical focus toward the symbolic, communicative, and anticipatory aspects of collective refusal, the concept of strike can be extended to capture emerging forms of digital resistance. This reframing preserves the political significance of strike while accommodating the transformed conditions of labour in the platform economy.

talks.title: Marxist Humanism: A Second Chance?
talks.abstract: Recently numerous publications appeared concerning the humanist Marx (not merely the young one!), his ethics of flourishing, and his ideas regarding democracy, republicanism, and nature. In light of this, I wish to address the question of whether these new interpretations hint at a revival of Marxist humanism. The earlier wave—inspired by, among others, Erich Fromm and the Yugoslav Praxis Group—was frequently derided as overly reformist and was discredited by Althusser’s polemics in the eyes of many. This time, however, things could be different; for today, humanism serves not so much to inspire moderation and compromise, but rather to radicalize the critique of a dehumanizing system. I therefore present a program outlining what Marxist humanism means for the 21st century. Concurrently, I would also like to briefly introduce a line of research examining the historical divergence between humanism and socialism in the Netherlands.

talks.title: What does prohibition prohibit? From the ideology to the communist pedagogy of drugs
talks.track: Social reproduction, care and Marxist feminism
talks.abstract: This presentation makes the case for why Marxists should engage drug culture and why we are uniquely positioned to do so – concretely, drugs and Marxism function as complementary educators in the materialism of social relations. It starts by analyzing the ideology of drug prohibition through the concept of “fetishism”, which it breaks down into assumptions of pharmacological reification, inherent danger, and illusion – the same rhetorical manoeuvres that discredit Marxism as dogmatic and utopian “gateway” to social degeneracy. While Marxist denunciations of the role of drugs as literal “opium of the people” have the advantage of shifting the critical target onto social relations, they have tended to reproduce this ideological schema and failed to go far enough into a consideration of the positive potential of drug culture. While all, including licit, drug use renders the materiality of capitalism’s psychic infrastructure tangible, here that certain forms of illicit recreational drug use belong to the sphere of social reproduction and contribute to the production of normative cultures that stand at odds with the dominant regimes of value under capitalism. Moreover, by sustaining cultures organized around values of sharing, caring, collectivity, autonomy, and pleasure, such forms of drug use promote postcapitalist forms of desire that should not be too easily dismissed as illusory or deradicalizing. Instead, the desire for drugs can be defetishized as a form of “baseline communism” and desire for communist social relations. This is not to derealize and indict the actually existing – and arguably ineradicable – desire for drugs, but to radicalize and think through it a thoroughly materialist manner. Conversely, drug use emerges not only as a crucial sociomaterial practice, but also as an educator in materiality - in the direct sense of how drug-matter affects consciousness, and in the broader sense in which (drug) experience is overdetermined by “set & setting” – one’s material context. From this point of view, drug prohibition is revealed as a prohibition of materialist thought and a communistic pedagogy of the senses. It is the retention of their illegal status along their disavowed wide availability that creates the reductive standpoint that views drugs as easy pleasures and forms of mindless escape offered by capitalism, when in fact what they reveal is that capitalism is not thoughtful or joyful enough. Thus, engaging with certain illegal drug pleasures is a clear chance to heighten the contradictions of living under capitalism rather than smoothening its function.

talks.title: ‘The way one digs up roots and dead bodies’: Not Forgetting Construction Grievances
talks.abstract:
For the avid reader of Marx, Sérgio Ferro, the history of architecture, viewed from the building site, is one of betrayals and defeats. Witnessing exploitative practices in Brasília under construction marks a departure for the then-young architect Sérgio Ferro from his design practice; he begins writing and joins the armed struggle against the dictatorship in Brazil in the 1960s. The paper engages with his writings, recently translated into English, paying closer attention to his hypothesis on self-management’s origins in the construction workers’ bitter emancipatory struggles on nineteenth-century building sites. It offers a comparative analysis of the contradiction of practicing architecture in the context of institutionalised self-management by situating another architect-in-resignation, Bogdan Bogdanović’s turn to the construction of partisan memorials in Yugoslavia and fascination with pre-modern heretic heritage. Neither of them, I argue, offers solutions for the contradiction that is contained in becoming an architect in self-management. But both are interested in memorialising the vanquished. 

Workers’ struggles on the building site are analysed through Ferro’s theorisation of ‘separated design’: the advancing demarcation between building execution and its organisation/management; capitalism’s tendency to detach manual from mental labour and historical circumstances of the emergence of the modern architect. That which appears melancholic in his critique is paradoxically also militant, by lingering on the self-inflicted violence of architectural design. The paper argues that Ferro’s attempt at ‘architecture from below’ brings self-management’s key demand — the reversal of the historical process of separation of intellectual and manual labour — in conjunction with architectural production as a radical approach to architectural history. It asks what it would mean for architecture if its praxis became attuned to the class struggle otherwise obscured, even repressed, by the normalisation of ‘separated design’, conjectured by Ferro.

talks.title: A Textual Research and Contemporary Interpretation of the Theory of "twofold character of production"
talks.abstract: In terms of sustaining the survival of human society, the production of the means of subsistence and the production of human beings themselves share a perpetually coexisting foundational status; in terms of shaping a specific social formation, which "production" occupies the dominant position is a dynamic historical process. This paper embeds the major practical proposition of "closely integrating investing in things and investing in people" into the classic theoretical horizon of the "twofold character of production", deeply analyzes the historical malady of Western capitalism, seeing things but not people, and highlighting the unique superiority of Chinese modernization.

talks.title: The Body That Refuses: PMOS and Carceral Embodiment
talks.track: Social reproduction, care and Marxist feminism
talks.abstract:
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is an endocrine disorder that extends beyond
biomedical diagnosis because of its social and cultural implications. Rather than treating
PMOS solely as a condition, I approach it as a mode of embodied experience through which
the contradictions of neoliberal femininity become materially visible. Under the current form
of capitalism, the female body becomes a site of optimisation and self-management. Women
are expected to be economically productive, reproductively capable, emotionally regulated,
and, on top of that, desirable. Health becomes framed not as a collective concern, but as an
individual responsibility achieved through discipline and self-surveillance. PMOS produces a
temporal form of confinement in which women are stuck between bodily unpredictability and
socially imposed reproductive timelines. Confinement becomes organised through delay and
anticipation, as the future becomes medically governed. Chronicity restructures everyday
existence because the illness is not experienced as a temporary interruption but a permanent
uncertainty requiring continuous self-improvement. Carcerality, in this case, emerges not
primarily through disciplinary institutions but through the endless labour required to sustain a
body that capitalism simultaneously depends upon and neglects. Drawing on
Marxist-feminist theories of social reproduction, I argue that PMOS exposes the limits of
neoliberal ideals of optimisation by rendering the body a site where productive, reproductive,
and affective labour can no longer be reconciled. Showcasing the need for an
anti-productivist restructuring of feminist politics of care, that center collective support and
the necessity of approaches attentive not only to symptoms but to women’s lived and social
experiences of illness. The goal shifts away from the capitalist need for constant regulation
toward sustainable coexistence with bodily instability. Women with PMOS frequently inhabit
bodies that cannot fully align with neoliberal timelines of productivity, career progression, or
reproduction, and rather than understanding this as failure, anti-productivist care requires
conditions under which unpredictable bodies remain livable and socially valued

talks.title: The consequences of aleatory materialism for revolutionary praxis.
talks.abstract:
ABSTRACT

In his final contribution to the marxian ‘science of history,’ the late Louis Althusser recasts history as a series of chance encounters in an attempt to rid historical materialism of all latent determinism and idealism. In doing so, communism becomes a fundamentally contingent possibility with a radically plural causal path. What remains of revolutionary praxis when history unfolds at the whims of chance?
Recoursing to Machiavelli, Althusser theorizes the history-making capacity present in humankind as the ability to produce a new Prince who, endowed with virtú, intervenes in fortuna. Revolutionary praxis becomes the cultivation of the capacity to act when a critical conjuncture, laden with the possibility of societal change, presents itself.

Shaking off idealisms, there can be no conception of the revolutionary subject as a world-historical person, a unified class, or a unified vanguard party driving class consciousness, nor can there be a reliance on pure spontaneism. Instead, a heterogeneous web of dispersed but more or less aligned movements must build the capacity to strike when fortuna presents itself, emphasizing ideological class struggle to produce ‘subjects of action.’

Drawing on the works of Althusser scholars like Tosel, Lahtinen, Morfino and Sotiris, who keep the question of revolutionary praxis deliberately open-ended, I sketch out a theory of practice. Anticipating the aleatory nature of a critical conjuncture, a revolutionary struggle must diversify its theaters of engagement such that whenever and wherever an encounter takes hold, organized capacity is present to act.
****

talks.title: Reading Marx
talks.abstract:
This paper asks why the uptake of value-form theory been so great among Marxist literary and cultural critics. As the editors of _After Marx: Literature, Theory, and Value_ have persuasively argued, recent years have seen a “collective rethinking of what a Marxist approach to literature might be and do,” one that responds to economic and cultural trends dating back to the 1960s. And yet, while a conjunctural analysis helps to clarify the disciplinary context, this paper addresses a more capacious conceptual overlap between aesthetic theory and value-form theory. The emphasis on form, for example, suggests an elective affinity between the two fields that hinges on modalities of reading. Emerging out of Adorno’s classroom at the Institute for Social Research in the 1960s, critics associated with the Neue Marx-Lektüre (NML) argued that the mode through which Marx presented his ideas, and the way in which we read him, are not secondary to but rather constitutive of the critique of political economy. By paying careful attention to Marx’s dialectical method, figures like Hans-Georg Backhaus were able to redress the mainstream Ricardian interpretation of Marx’s mature project, which misrepresented it as “one economic theory besides many others”.

As Michael Heinrich has argued, disentangling the “hidden logic” and “inner coherence” of Marx’s writings requires going beyond the published version of his presentation and uncritically digesting its contents. Rather, because Marx redrafted his value-form analysis across reams of preparatory notes and throughout successive editions of _Capital_, readers must adopt a hermeneutical approach of textual reconstruction not dissimilar to the kind of comparative methodologies taught in university literature departments. To maintain fidelity to Marx is thus to read him with alertness and suspicion, creativity and commitment, hence the quasi-deconstructionist fanaticism of value-form theory, its reverence for the text. This idea of Marxism as an open-ended and unfinished project places agency back into the hands of readers and interpreters of Marx, whose role becomes one of active theoretical production, not passive reception. In this spirit, this paper proposes returning to Marx in order to rediscover him anew, intervening in critical conversations surrounding his mature critique and its capacity to generate fresh lines of inquiry into aesthetics and culture.

talks.title: The Commune: a Perspective for Socialism in the 21st Century
talks.abstract:
The spiral of crises caused by the capitalist system has dragged us into a succession of genocides, femicides, ecocides, attacks against life and against society. As this system drives itself towards its end, it is up to us to determine if this end will also mean the end of humanity, or if before and from it can different and alternative forms of life emerge. 
Capitalist Modernity is the last 500 years of a much longer system of oppression that started with the oppression against women and the society built around women. Various characteristics distinguish Capitalist Modernity from the previous forms of oppression, and between them one stands out: “society (…) was opened up to influence, invasion, and colonization by the power apparatus in all of its most hidden nooks and crannies”. (Öcalan, 2020, 351) This development has allowed the power apparatus to condition every relationship, to limit the ability of people to imagine, and in this sense the ability to create. 
Antonio Gramsci, in an era more similar to today that we might want to admit, has grasped this concept with his analysis on cultural hegemony, and the consequent need for subaltern classes, to imagine, create and live an own cultural and political reality. The resistance against hegemony and oppression has historically taken different forms: from rebellions and revolts, to the forms of “Everyday Communism” described by David Graeber, as an heritage of relationships based on human solidarity. 
The connection between these experiences and forms of everyday resistance, as well as the need to not only go against but also go beyond the domination that surrounds us, are central in the new Manifesto for a Democratic Communal Society (2026), through which Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement open their proposals, their experiences of struggle in the Rojava Revolution and all the other parts of Kurdistan, to the Middle East and to the whole world.
Central in this new perspective is the Commune, as a form of social organizing taken historically by society, that often appears as the most natural form of organization for the experiences of resistance to this system. To consciously live and recreate this form of life, and to strengthen its already existing aspects, while always looking for solutions to problems, might be what can allow us to end this continuous cycle of crises through an alternative form of life, a free life for everyone, everywhere.

talks.title: Ton Korver. Alle Tijd. Marx over een economie die ons tijd belooft maar tijd ontneemt
talks.abstract: The last book by the late Dutch economist and sociologist Ton Korver presents a clear and sophisticated case for the importance and continuing relevance of the economic theory of Karl Marx, as opposed to the theories of the neoclassical school, still prevailing in the academias all over the world. In this highly original book, Ton Korver enters the real fray, not with dogmatic Marxism but with the concept of economics dominant in the real world of capitalism today.

talks.title: Considerations on Online Maoism
talks.abstract: This presentation will discuss the legacy of Maoism on contemporary digital culture. Maoism, or Mao Zedong Thought, exercised a pronounced influence on radical movements and thought in the West, particularly among Black liberation struggles in the US and in anti-imperialist currents in the New Left of the 1960s and ‘70s. This influence was not due to any kind of strategy of the Chinese Communist Party, but happened in ways we would today recognize as grassroots and “viral”: primarily through the decentralized dissemination of Quotations from Chairman Mao (the so-called “Little Red Book”). Maoism’s emphasis on ideological struggle and cultural revolution was attractive to the counterculture, and led to distinct cultural expressions. As Maoism receded politically along with the New Left, it remained a consistent undercurrent in activist circles, and would eventually find its way online through e-zines and discussion boards. In the 21st Century, as American imperialism took an aggressive new form, Maoism was rediscovered by a new generation, and has been incorporated into a variety of meme formats and online slang terminology. The goal of this presentation is to begin to think through what happens when Marxism goes online, and is metabolized through the genres and practices that characterize digital media.

talks.title: Settler Capital: Investing in the Dispossession of Munsee Land, 1620-1780
talks.abstract: Recent work under the heading of settler/colonial/racial capitalism incorporates valuable insights from settler-colonial theory and critical Indigenous theory into political economy. However, these adjectivized capitalisms have produced a blurry landscape of overlapping concepts that at times glosses over the specific workings of capital as a circulation of value. I offer the concept of settler capital as a more operational analytic, defined as the dual process of investing in dispossession and commodifying settlement. Settler capital mobilizes value toward the severing of Indigenous relations to land and the creation of commodity markets in real property for sale to populations of settlers. I examine two Early Modern proprietary ventures in Munsee Lenape territory—New Netherland patroonships and the West Jersey Society—to sketch the early genealogy and elementary structures of settler capital in North America that were inherited by the political economy of the United States. From this perspective, frontlines of dispossession are only one, albeit essential, material bottleneck in a wider circulation of value that begins and ends elsewhere in space and time, whether in the Amsterdam boardrooms of the Dutch West India Company or the London offices of the West Jersey Society. Global circulations of value contribute inertia to racialized violence as Indigenous relations to land are posited as friction to settler capital’s self-realization. Specifying settler capitalists interests in this way supports the argument that, after the Proclamation of 1763, possibilities of Indigenous sovereignty pushed many American investors in land companies toward the revolutionary project of settler statecraft.

talks.title: Big Tech and cost of living: Marx' antinomy of social reproduction
talks.abstract: From his early 1844 Manuscripts or his later “Fragment on Machines” in the Grundrisse to his mature volumes of Capital, Karl Marx has consistently stressed the role of technology in capitalist domination. These criticisms have recently returned with the rise of Artificial Intelligence in the workplace, which not only threatens workers with mass unemployment but also risks subjugating the workers who remain in employment under tight managerial surveillance. Marx expressed similar worries about industrial technological development during the 19th century. He described how new steam-powered productions methods were transforming the world of work in favour of capital accumulation and to the detriment of worker autonomy and wellbeing. However, his critique shifts and turns across multiple lines of thought. As Sandro Mezzadra argues in Nei cantieri marxiani (2014), Marx’s oeuvre is composed of many “workshops” (cantieri), conceptual experiments that Marx develops and drops again every time he starts writing a new draft. Marx scholarship has subsequently attempted to synthesize these multiple critical experiments into a consistent critical theory of technology. Some highlight the problem of alienation as key to Marx’ concerns about capitalist technology (Marcuse, Feenberg, Wendling), others stress the erosion of worker autonomy by separating control and execution over the labour process (Braverman, Panzieri, Pasquinelli), and yet others highlight the tendencies of modern technologies to wear human bodies and minds out beyond their natural limits (Rabinbach, Saito, Berardi). However, less attention has been granted to imagining better, communist technologies or AI more specifically. Most efforts have focused on the few paragraphs in the “Fragment on Machines” that promise a post-work liberation from labour through mass automation. However, Marx only briefly mentioned this option in one draft text and abandoned the option immediately afterwards. This choice should make us question Marx’s resolve for a “fully automated luxury communism” (Bastani) and look for alternative modes of worker-centric technological development. What institutions can reconcile new technologies like AI with worker desires for autonomy and wellbeing? What technologies would result from such a revolution in technological design? In this paper, I will conduct a historical-reconstructive reading of Marx’ notebooks between specifically the writing of the Grundrisse in 1857-58 and Capital: Volume I in 1867 to extract his positive proposals for worker-centric technology and its implications for AI development.

talks.title: Prestige Literature in the Protest Decade: Ben Lerner and the Crisis of Liberalism in the 2010s
talks.abstract:
This paper uses a Marxist approach to argue that Ben Lerner’s autofiction illuminates the intense contradictions of 2010s US liberalism. Whereas contemporary US literary studies often draws homologies between literary form and the institutional circumstances of its production, I argue that larger forces of history, class struggle, and ideology determined the form and content of this prestigious body of work. The homology I draw out is between ramshackle literary form and liberalism in crisis.

Lerner’s autofiction was part of a recent cultural moment that evaporated quickly, in the U.S. in the late 2010s. Liberalism was beset by economic, political, and climate crisis—but the mood was hopeful. Large bottom-up social movements, from Occupy to BLM, characterized the decade. Literature and public intellectualism enjoyed an upturn in prestige, crystallized in the juggernaut careers of the writers my dissertation studies: Jesmyn Ward, Viet Thanh Nguyen, Maggie Nelson, and Lerner. This diverse group was united by their receiving the consecration and patronage of the MacArthur Fellowships, alongside contemporaries like Lin-Manuel Miranda, Ta-Nehisi Coates, Nikole-Hannah Jones, and Claudia Rankine.

Lerner’s novels illuminate a remarkable feature of dominant US culture in the mid-to-late 2010s, in that they are _committed literature_; writing that, in Sartre’s conception, contributes to political struggle, rather than merely representing it. Critics acknowledge Lerner’s work is political but understate its radicalism. It is utopian and anti-capitalist. But if Lerner’s fiction was so radical, why would an elite institution like the MacArthurs celebrate it, awarding Lerner the “genius grant” in 2015? I show Lerner’s canonization fit into a larger adaptation of American liberalism to radical energies and materialist critiques. Absent a powerful, organized American Left, what 2010s committed literature most contributed to was the shoring up liberalism.

talks.title: Thermodynamic Marx: The Conservation of Value
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract:
This presentation probes a counterintuitive question: What if there was no growth of value in the capitalist economy? What if value was instead conserved? In the natural sciences, the core intuition that properties are conserved springs up in a multitude of fields. There are principles governing the conservation of momentum, spin, and famously, energy. Such principles have traveled to the humanities and social sciences, too, as in the case of Sigmund Freud’s insight that desire can be repressed and sublimated but not destroyed or with Chantal Mouffe’s thesis that “the political” can be driven underground but never extinguished. Classical political economy, too, was influenced by mechanical principles of conservation, as Philip Mirowski has shown. In Marx’s writings, this paper argues, one finds multiple principles of conservation that finally amount to the philosophical presupposition that value remains conserved under capitalism.

The argument works as follows. Value, for Marx, is above all a historically specific political relation. This political relation is the class struggle between labor-power and capital, which provides the historical constant of capitalism. Since all value ultimately originates in this political relation, labor-power must be exploited more intensively to increase society’s throughput of “wealth” and “worth”, its flows of biophysical matter-energy and money. It is a dynamic that Moishe Postone has termed capitalism’s “treadmill effect”. The laws of value now become the inverse of the laws of energy. Whereas energy always remains conserved, while being increasingly unable to do work; value remains always conserved, while doing more and more work. This inversion surfaces as capital’s ecological contradiction. Value, as a political relation that is conserved under capitalism, is split between a negentropic drive toward the maximization of wealth and its entropic drive toward the maximization of waste.

talks.title: Changing tack, from the defence towards designing a novel future
talks.abstract:
A Historical Materialist worldview entails two basic elements: a) the study how and why our society and its mechanisms developed as we experience them here and now, b) the study of the immanent tensions of our present society and quest how to transcend our ‘dying culture’ into a —further to be sketched — socialist society. 
This brings us to reevaluate old discussions on our capabilities of futuristic designs beyond moral and romantic utopian dreams of ideal societies. In particular the directions and use of science and technology and the suggestions that technologies are ‘neutral’ and sciences are ever more comprehensive. On the one hand we have the difficult, but actually low hanging fruits, of to what extent e.g. statistical methods as in AI, or technologies such as nuclear energy can be reprocessed in a not-capitalist, preferably ‘socialist’  society, and on the other hand how our present-day limited scientific theories and models, which are convolutions of our sensory and mental make-up as humans and their expressions in a particular socio-economic system.
An interesting historical case was the discussions between the Marxist Vladimir Lenin and the Emperiomonist positivist Alexander Bogdanov,  on the issue of (adult) education and the notion of a distinct _Proletarian Science_, prior to the establishment of a post revolutionary culture. After a century the works of Bogdanov are now properly translated into English, which allows further scrutiny.
Bogdanov’s wrote his fourteen theses: ‘_Science and the Working Class’_ in advance of his presentation on 17 September 1918 to the First All-Russian Conference of the Proletkult organisations held in Moscow, September 1918.
He developed the idea that, as the proletariat is the class that will topple and overcome capitalism, the proletariat will also be the source of a novel culture in which people will work in a comradely and collectivist way, developing a unified science encompassing all human knowledge. Bogdanov situates this Proletarian Science as a political conscious possibility in conjunction with the revolution. This in contradistinction with Lenin, who emphasises the priority of the political, hence social, “regime change”.  It is important to note that Bogdanov’s approach is based on the latest developments in industrialisation and culminates in his system theoretical universal theory of Tektology. A theory based on the search for equilibria ‘overcoming’ all notions of dialectical progress.

talks.title: Our Chronopolitics: Marxism, Literary History, and Millennial Socialism
talks.abstract:
This paper focuses on a specific episode in the academic culture of North American universities in the period after the 2008 financial crisis, but touches on larger issues of Marxist intellectual history, political economy, and generational politics. Mark McGurl’s 2009 book _The Program Era_ profoundly shaped the work of a generation of literary scholars in the United States and abroad. Combining Jamesonian literary and ideological analysis with a sweeping historical account of the rise of creative writing programs as the preeminent institution shaping postwar U.S. fiction, it was the signature work of a rejuvenated literary sociology, or what has been called, sometimes disparagingly, 'New Institutionalism’ (NI). Emphatically focused on the explanatory power of 'mid-level' contexts, NI drew heavily on French sociology (Bourdieu, Latour) but has had an ambiguous relationship to the Marxist tradition. It has also proved popular with audiences beyond academic literary studies, resulting in a number of ‘crossover’ books attracting public attention. Taking a page from NI methods, I argue that both its aesthetic strategies and its ideological limitations are best explained as complex responses to particular historical and institutional conditions.

NI was a writing practice that developed within specific intellectual, political, and labor conditions in U.S. universities in the 1990s, which only intensified after the 2008 Great Recession. These included declining enrollments in the English major amid a broader crisis in ‘literary’ reading, profound changes in university labor relations, and the rise of left- and right-wing challenges to neoliberal governance. Focusing on the style and sensibility of two major, recent works--McGurl’s _Everything and Less_ (2021) and Dan Sinykin’s _Big Fiction_ (2023)--I argue that, at its best, NI has performed a valuable mediation of Marxism for an audience that includes scholars and other highly educated service workers, radicalized by diminishing career and life prospects. Characteristic features of NI, including some of its stylistic 'tics,' should be understood in terms of a broader project of raising class consciousness in a period of widespread disillusionment with liberal capitalist institutions—including the novel and the university—and rising authoritarianism. Cutting across some of its generational and sectarian rivalries, this paper helps situate the Institutional Turn in literary studies within a long tradition of Left intellectual production in Anglo-American universities. It also prompts reflection on the intellectual consequences of our own profoundly unsettled institutional context in the present.

talks.title: Revisiting the Anti-Ecological Treadmill of Capitalism
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract:
Despite recent economic developments, such as financialisation and the rise of service sectors, commodity production remains integral to the capitalist world economy and a crucial driver of ecological degradation. This presentation revisits different uses of the concept of the 'Treadmill' in Marxian theory to explain capital's anti-ecological tendency to accelerate commodity production and material throughput at an ever-increasing rate. 

Accordingly, this presentation first discusses Moishe Postone’s use of the treadmill concept in his Time, Labour, and Social Domination. For Postone, a temporal ‘treadmill’ dynamic emerges from capital’s law of value. In his exegesis of Capital, Postone shows how firms can obtain competitive advantages and profits by increasing labour productivity and producing more commodities in less time. This allows firms to offer comparatively cheaper products because these products contain less labour time. A treadmill emerges when others catch up on these productivity gains, requiring firms to make new productivity investments with which competitors eventually catch up, which requires a new round of investments, etc. Not only does this accelerate production times, but it also expands the mass of goods produced as well as resources extracted and waste produced as a necessary result thereof. 
           
Subsequently, this presentation moves to the Treadmill of Production (ToP) theory developed in Marxian environmental sociology to embed this treadmill dynamic between capitalist competitors in a broader sociopolitical context. ToP theorists, affirming the abovementioned dynamics, further show how labour movements and governments are also compelled to support the expansion of productive capacities. Perhaps more interestingly, they show how treadmill tendencies generate various political and economic crises that are, paradoxically, resolved through further expansions of production and material throughput. As such, the ToP emphasises a widespread, self-proliferating growth dependency that intensifies an extractive and dysfunctional relation with both human and more-than-human nature.  
            
Crucially, this presentation argues, treadmill theories also highlight the futility of expanding production. Both Postone and ToP theorists highlight how socioeconomic benefits, for capitalists or societies at large, of increased productivity are temporary and defeated by capital’s own dynamics. Not only do treadmill tendencies drive ecological degradation, then, but they also do so without benefitting societies – and working-class people specifically – in the long run. In explaining this, I thus argue that returning to the notion of the treadmill can help us explain and critique capital’s anti-ecological tendencies.

talks.title: Mobilising contemporary Marxism to organise post-capitalist transformation
talks.abstract:
This paper interrogates contemporary post-capitalist thought through the lens of the ongoing Marxist renaissance. While post-capitalism has emerged as a prominent horizon for social movements since the 1990s, from the Zapatista Army of National Liberation to Occupy Wall Street, it has frequently been articulated through anti-foundational and prefigurative approaches that remain skeptical of strategic orientation and institutional transformation grounded in the reorganization of material relations. In critical organization studies, this has generated a growing literature on alternative organizations, cooperatives, democratic organizing and community economies that fails to adequately theorize how such initiatives relate to capitalist totality and systemic transformation.

We argue that much of this literature implicitly assumes that the survival and diffusion of new forms of economic organization will gradually lead to their 'spilling over' into capitalism, organically triggering broader societal change. Such assumptions however underestimate capitalism’s historical coexistence with non-capitalist organisational forms and its inherent dependence, for its own reproduction, upon its constitutive ‘outsides:’ unpaid reproductive labour, commons, racialized extraction, subsistence economies, and ecological appropriation. The transformative potential of new forms of economic organizing depends, we argue, on how they articulate with broader struggles over accumulation, social reproduction, state power, racial capitalism and ecological crisis.

To address this problem, the paper mobilizes seven contemporary strands of Marxism - Community Economies, Autonomist Marxism, Analytical Marxism, Open Marxism, Social Reproduction Theory, Black Marxism, and Degrowth Communism - to theorize post-capitalist transformation. We understand these perspectives as distinct efforts to renew Marx’s critique of political economy under contemporary conditions marked by socio-ecological crisis and the disorganization of oppressed communities. Together, these approaches illuminate different dimensions of capitalist domination and possibilities for rupture.

Rather than abandoning Marxist assumptions, the paper argues that critical organization studies need to recover them through the Marxist renaissance in relation to multiple contemporary struggles on class, race, gender, and ecology, as well as how to organize and strategize for post-capitalist transformation.  Post-capitalist transformation is conceptualized not as the automatic outcome of organizational diffusion, nor as the realization of a predetermined historical trajectory, but as a contradictory and politically contested process of diffuse organizing emerging within and against capitalist social relations. 

The paper concludes by outlining a research agenda for Marxist organization studies that is attentive to crisis, (de)mediation, totality, and transformative strategy, beyond localistic prefigurative politics and economistic determinism.

talks.title: Heroism and the Left in Times of Disaster Nationalism
talks.abstract: This paper asks how the left has historically understood heroism and poses the question of how it might understand it today at a moment of climate breakdown and an ascendant far right. Following Alain Badiou´s exposition of “The Figure of the Soldier” in his Philosophy For Militants (2012), particular focus is put the figure of the armed hero. The paper traces Fredric Jameson’s discussion of the iconic image of Che Guevara in his periodisation of the 1960s through to Zapatismo’s explicit rejection of the figure of the Guevarist insurrectionary by the 1990s, and extends the historicization of thinking about the armed hero on the left to interventions today by figures on the radical left, from Andreas Malm to Jodi Dean, Enzo Traverso and Gilbert Achcar. In drawing out and comparing these various strands of thought, particular emphasis is put on three questions: first, Badiou’s posing of the figure of the armed hero as emblematic of times of disorientation; second, Traverso’s critique of contemporary memory culture that valorizes the memory of victims rather than the memory of the vanquished; and finally, the question of how the figure of the hero connects to the theorization of violence and praxis on the left, as posed by historical and contemporary figures, ranging from Lenin to Fanon to Balibar.

talks.title: Embracing Environmental Alienation in Eco-Marxist Politics
talks.track: The ecological crisis: class and climate
talks.abstract:
Eco-socialists and Marxist political ecologists owe much to Marx. His historical materialist method embodies its own ecological materialism insofar as he understood natural and human history as two sides of the same coin; and theorists have taken up the concept of metabolic rift to analyse today’s intensifying ecological crises. What interests me, however, is the implicit idea in eco-Marxist (and critical and not-so-critical environmental) thought that *alienation* from nature must be overcome as part of a necessary change in our metabolic relationship with the more-than-human world. 

In his book *Embracing Alienation: Why We Shouldn't Try to Find Ourselves* Todd McGowan argues that the negativity associated with alienation is a direct result of the success of Marx’s account of the concept over Hegel’s. Though only implicit in *Capital* after a more enthusiastic treatment in the *Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844*, Marx’s thinking about alienation is a throughline in his critique of capital, which creates a society in which people relate to each other through the meditation of the (ecologically costly) commodity. This entails a loss for humanity and impetus for overcoming capitalism in order to bridge the gap it introduces between the subject and the environment.

I will land on the Hegelian side of the debate over alienation. Hegel understands alienation as positive – the path to emancipation for the subject – and as I will argue, for the (eco)social. While I will endorse Marx’s analysis of the alienation of the worker from the product of their labour and the environment, I will show how embracing the unpleasant truth of an always-alienated relationship to the natural world is an inherent characteristic of social existence. What’s more, doubling down on this insight from German idealism and psychoanalysis has the potential to repoliticise ecological politics. If an unalienated, harmonious integration with nature is impossible, we are forced to choose which socio-natural relationships to create and nurture. It is hence from this point that eco-socialist politics should start.
